activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Deliberate practice means working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, which improves skill more than simply playing through pieces already known.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and cold concrete, and Joseph had claimed it as his own since September, when his mother stopped parking inside and the old lawnmower went to the curb. He sat on an overturned milk crate with his grandfather's trumpet, which had come to him dented and green at the seams, and he played the same eight bars of a Chet Baker line he already knew. He played them well, or well enough. When he finished, Tobias, who had come over to escape his own house and its renovation dust, applauded from a folding chair with a bag of chips balanced on his knee.

"You've played that exact thing maybe forty times," Tobias said. "I counted while I was eating."

"It's called warming up."

"It's called hiding." Tobias brushed salt off his jeans. His real errand, Joseph suspected, was the one he'd been circling for weeks: the school jazz combo needed a trumpet player by November, and Tobias, who played bass and organized everything from the yearbook to the lunch table's seating, wanted him to audition. "Mr. Balogun runs it," Tobias said, as if the name were a credential. "He lives two doors down, the one with the drums in his garage. You should just go."

Through the open garage door, in the slant of late afternoon, Joseph could actually see Mr. Balogun's place, its own door lifted, and hear the same thing he'd heard every evening that week: a girl playing piano, then stopping, then playing the same phrase again, then a man's voice, low and unhurried, cutting in. On Friday, curious and a little circumspect about eavesdropping, Joseph walked his trumpet down the sidewalk under the pretense of taking out the trash.

Kassandra from his chemistry class was at the upright piano that filled half of Mr. Balogun's garage. She had been playing something bright and complete sounding, a pop song she clearly loved, and she had played it three times through while he sat on a stool with his arms folded. When she started it a fourth time he raised one hand, gentle, and she stopped mid-chord.

"The one you like, you already know," Mr. Balogun said. "Give me the two bars you keep avoiding instead." He set a metronome ticking on the piano lid. "Six times, slow, and listen to each one."

Joseph lingered at the trash cans longer than trash required. He watched Kassandra grimace, play the two bars, miss, play them again. Mr. Balogun said only "closer" or "the third note," short as a coin dropped on a counter. She had a clear goal each attempt and a verdict immediately after, and the ugly little passage began, grudgingly, to straighten itself out. When she finally got it clean twice in a row, she laughed the way people laugh when they've been holding their breath.

"Tobias says you're joining combo," she said, spotting him. "He told the whole chem table you're a prodigy."

"Tobias exaggerates for sport."

She rolled her shoulders. "Those two bars were ruining the whole song for me. I just kept playing the fun part instead." She said it like a confession, and Joseph, standing there with his trumpet case sweating in his hand, felt the same confession arrange itself inside him without wanting to.

Back in his own garage that evening, he laid the trumpet out and, for the first time, made a taxonomy of what he could and couldn't do: the eight known bars in one column, and beneath them, honestly, the high F that cracked, the phrase that always rushed, the transition he faked by breathing through. He picked the cracked F. He set his phone metronome to sixty, played the note, listened, played it again. It failed. He adjusted his jaw, tried again; it failed differently, less badly. Tobias appeared in the doorway somewhere around the eleventh attempt, chewing, watching without comment, and Joseph was faintly aware of him the way you're aware of weather, pleasant and beside the point.

On the twenty-somethingth try the note came out round and full, and it extruded through the garage and out the open door into the dark, startling a cat off the fence. Joseph played it once more to be sure, and it held.

"Was that it?" Tobias said.

"That was it. Sixty more to go, probably."

Tobias dragged the folding chair to the door and sat down. "So you'll audition?"

Joseph wiped the mouthpiece on his sleeve, considering how much he didn't yet know, how many cracked notes stood between him and a stage. "Friday," he said. "You're counting my attempts."

"Someone has to keep the stats," Tobias said, unwrapping a second bag of chips. "Number twelve was rough, by the way."

"Number twelve was rough," Joseph agreed, and raised the trumpet again.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections.
story:
The pharmacy smelled of cardboard and hand sanitizer, and Connor stood in aisle three holding his phone like evidence. Griffin was meeting him here in ten minutes, before the walk-in clinic on Marsh Street closed at six, and Connor had promised, in a text he had typed and deleted twice, that he would explain what to say at the desk, what to ask for, what the swab involved. He was eighteen and had never done this himself. Two months ago he had sat through a health assembly meant to inculcate responsibility into the senior class, and while everyone around him whispered, he had written down the clinic's hours.

Griffin came through the automatic doors with his hands in his pockets. "I leave tomorrow morning," he said. "So this is today or never."

"This is today. We've got forty minutes."

At the counter, a girl from their grade was waiting, and it took Connor a second to recognize Abigail, out of context, in the fluorescent light. She had a white paper bag and a prescription slip, and she was asking the pharmacist a question in a voice pitched low, the way people talk about things they have decided not to be embarrassed about but still are. Connor, pretending to read the back of a vitamin bottle three feet away, heard most of it.

"So the pill," Abigail said. "It covers me, right? Like, everything?"

Mr. Schneider, gray-haired, unhurried, set the bag down. "It's very good at preventing pregnancy. It does nothing against infections. If you want something that does both, the only common method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections is a condom. The pill and a condom are doing two different jobs."

"Oh." Abigail looked at the bag as if it had changed weight. "Nobody said that part."

"Nobody usually does," said Mr. Schneider, and slid a small box of condoms across the counter without ceremony, the way a person passes the salt.

Connor turned back to Griffin, and something rearranged itself in him. He had spent the drive here rehearsing a speech about the clinic, about testing, about how asking was the brave part, and the speech now seemed both too small and too large. The fact he had overheard was so plain. Two jobs, two methods, one overlap. He had assumed, without ever examining the assumption, that protection was a single switch you flipped.

"Okay," he said. "Here's the actual plan, not the assembly version." He walked Griffin toward the family planning shelf, out of Abigail's earshot. "At the clinic you say you want a full screen. They ask if you want to talk about contraception, and you say yes, because it's free and they know things. And whatever happens with anyone, ever, the rule is the other person has to actually want it, out loud, and can change their mind halfway through. Not a hint. Not silence. Not because you're both already in the room."

Griffin picked up a box, turned it over, put it back. "Did you learn this somewhere or make it up?"

"Both, I think. The clinic part I got from their website. The other part I got from being confused for a long time and finally deciding what I actually believe." Connor shrugged. "I'm still not sure how you tell wanting from not minding. That part, I'm figuring out."

Abigail appeared beside them, her bag under her arm, her cheeks still pink. "I wasn't eavesdropping," she said, which was clearly a lie in both directions. "Do you two know where the clinic is? My mom thinks I'm at the library."

Connor's volition, which had faltered at the counter and again in aisle three, settled into something steadier. "Marsh Street. It closes at six. We're walking there now." He looked at Griffin, then at her, and added, without planning to, "You can come with us. Nobody there asks who you are."

They went out into the late light together, Griffin carrying the box of condoms he had circled back for, Abigail walking half a step ahead as though the pace belonged to her. Behind them the automatic doors exhaled a melancholic little sigh and closed. At the corner, Connor checked his phone. Twenty-six minutes.

"Run?" said Abigail, and she was already moving.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate.
story:
Sophie had claimed the table by the window on the second floor of the public library, the one with a view of the creek that ran behind the parking lot, because she liked watching the water while her brain overheated. Spread in front of her were the photocopies Ms. Somsak had made: a mock petition, a pretend high school's dress code, and the assignment sheet for the mock court, which required each student to argue both sides of a free speech case before a panel of teachers. Sophie was to be the school's lawyer for ten minutes and the students' lawyer for ten minutes after that, and she had no idea yet how a person could believe two opposite things in one afternoon without becoming a fraud.

Simon dropped into the chair across from her and set down a bag of cheese curls, which was against library rules, and which he clearly knew. "I'm here for the free speech case," he said. "Gillian's meeting us at four. She wants the students' side to win so badly she's already written a chant."

"The case isn't about winning," Sophie said. "It's about arguing both sides."

"That's the dialectic, right?" Simon said, licking orange dust off one finger. "Thesis, antithesis, whatever. Ms. Somsak loves that stuff. Say the word dialectic in your opening and she'll probably faint."

Sophie had already found the heart of her problem. The mock case involved a student, suspended for wearing an armband to protest the paving of the riparian greenway beside the school's creek, and the school defending its dress code on the grounds of order. When she searched through Ms. Somsak's packet for the most famous line about student speech, she found it in a footnote, and it was better than anything she could have invented. "Listen to this," she said, and read aloud. "In Tinker v. Des Moines, 1969, the Supreme Court ruled seven to two that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate."

"So the school loses," Simon said through a mouthful. "Done. Can we go?"

"Seven to two," Sophie said. "Not nine to zero. Two justices thought the school was right. And Tinker was about armbands worn quietly, and our case is an armband too, but the school says this one disrupted a fundraiser." She spread the two photocopies side by side and tried to interpolate the old ruling into her new facts, sliding the 1969 decision between the lines of the mock petition the way the creek slid between the riparian willows outside. The fit was not clean. That was the part nobody had warned her about: the law was a bridge you built while standing on it.

Gillian arrived at four with a poster she had made in advance of a verdict, which read STUDENTS HAVE RIGHTS in letters so large they were visible from the reference desk. The librarian came over and asked, in the politest possible voice, whether the poster could be folded, and Gillian folded it with the wounded dignity of someone whose protest had been suppressed for the second time that week. "I'm just saying," Gillian said, sitting down, "if they can suspend a guy for a piece of felt on his arm, then nothing means anything."

"Meaning isn't the same as winning," Sophie said, and immediately regretted how it sounded, like a fortune cookie. She tried again. "When I argue the school's side, I think I'll say the schoolhouse gate goes both ways. Rights pass through it, but so does the school's responsibility for the hundred kids at that fundraiser."

"Boo," said Gillian, but quietly, because they were in a library, and being against shushing was different from being shushed.

For an hour they took turns playing the panel. Simon, who had wanted only to finish his cheese curls and go home, discovered a genuine talent for judicial cruelty, interrupting Sophie mid-sentence to say "Counsel, the Court is unmoved" and "Counsel, the Court is falling asleep." Gillian argued the students' side with a fluency that startled Sophie, pointing out that a seven to two ruling meant the country itself had been divided, that the two dissenting justices had not been monsters, and that this was exactly why the school board should hesitate before suspending a boy with a felt band on his arm. Sophie wrote down one of Gillian's sentences almost word for word, because it was better than hers, and told her so, and Gillian went pink and pretended to reorganize the poster.

When the library announced it was closing, they packed up slowly. Sophie still did not know which side she actually believed, and she understood, walking past the reference desk with the folded poster under her arm, that she might never know, and that this might be what Ms. Somsak meant by preparation. At the door, Simon held up his empty cheese curl bag like a trophy. "For the record," he said, "I ate contraband snacks in a government building all afternoon, and nobody suspended me."

"That's because you have no message," Gillian said. "You can't censor nothing."

Sophie laughed, and outside, in the parking lot above the dark creek, she realized the banner for the riparian greenway was strung across the walking bridge where she'd left it that morning, and the city had already hung its construction permit directly beneath it, the two of them rippling together over the water like arguments waiting their turn.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: In October 2024 the Los Angeles Times did not endorse a presidential candidate after its owner blocked the editorial board's plans, and several board members resigned in protest.
story:
The library smelled like floor wax and old bindings, and David had claimed the corner table by the periodicals since fourth period, spreading drafts of the editorial like evidence at a trial. The piece reported that the district had quietly shifted sixty thousand dollars from the music program into the new stadium scoreboard, using budget documents he had requested three times before anyone answered. Principal's office had not said pull it. They had said postpone it, which he understood was the same request wearing a nicer shirt.

Edgar dropped his backpack on the opposite chair and slid a printed email across the table. "From Mr. Pham. He's the adviser now, apparently. Interim." The email was two sentences long. It reminded David that the paper represented the school, that timing mattered, and that a responsible editor considered whether a story served readers or merely attention. David read it twice. He had expected the assistant principal, the athletics booster who called the old scoreboard "an embarrassment" at every meeting. He had not expected Mr. Pham, who had once told their journalism class that a newspaper's only boss was the reader.

"That's not a reason," David said. "That's a dysphemism for don't. He's dressing it up so it sounds like maturity." Edgar shrugged with the insouciant calm of someone who would graduate in June no matter what the paper printed, and David envied him for it. Two years of chasing hall quotes and retracted lunch rumors had not inured David to the feeling of being managed. Each small deflection still landed like the first one.

Caleigh arrived with her laptop already open, which meant she had been reading about it. "You know this isn't original," she said, sitting down. "Last October. The Los Angeles Times. Their editorial board was going to endorse a presidential candidate, and the paper's owner blocked them, so the paper ran no endorsement at all. Some of the board members resigned over it. Actual journalists, quitting actual jobs." She turned the screen toward him. David read the story slowly, the way he read anything he suspected he would need later.

"So the owner gets what he wants," Edgar said, "and the paper looks like it just decided to stay neutral. Neutral and silenced look identical from outside."

"Except to the people who quit," Caleigh said.

David leaned back and looked at the ceiling tiles, which were water-stained in a pattern he had never bothered to map. Part of him wanted the grand version: print the editorial anyway, get Mr. Pham removed as adviser, become the boy who would not fold. But that version had him deciding who Mr. Pham was on the basis of one email, and he remembered the day in journalism class when Mr. Pham had defended a student's right to print a story about mold in the gym, against the same assistant principal, and won. People got squeezed. Owners got squeezed. Maybe it mattered less what a person was than where they stood when pressure arrived, and pressure arrived everywhere eventually.

"Here's what we can do," David said finally, pulling the drafts back into a stack. "We don't postpone and we don't defy. We publish, but we publish the email with it. The whole thing, exactly as sent. If the administration thinks the timing is a mistake, readers can judge the timing and the budget both. We're not calling anyone a censor. We're just not hiding the hand on the scale." He tapped the page. "The Times didn't run an endorsement and everyone found out why anyway. The finding out is the part that matters. The resignations made the silence louder than an endorsement would have been."

Caleigh was already copying the email into the layout file. Edgar read the new headline over her shoulder, "District Moves Music Money; Editor Advised to Wait," and gave a low whistle. "You realize they'll be furious that you quoted them."

"They'll be furious either way," David said. "At least this way they're furious about something true." He saved the file twice, then a third time to a drive in his pocket, because he had learned that much about timing himself.

They stayed until the lights over the periodicals clicked to half brightness and the librarian began wheeling her cart toward the exits. Mr. Pham was at the circulation desk, checking out a stack of books with his faculty card, and he looked up as they passed. David stopped, held out the printed layout, and waited while the older man read it in silence.

"Well," Mr. Pham said, handing it back. "You'll need to fix the spacing on page two."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: In Canadian federal elections, an eligible voter who is not on the voters list can register at their assigned polling place on election day.
story:
Alexander woke on election morning with the small, formal weight of a first ballot somewhere in his chest, and by the time he was buttering toast he had thought to wonder whether the voters list even knew he existed. He had turned eighteen in March, twelve days after the writ dropped, and somewhere in the shuffle of midterms and his grandmother's funeral he could not remember filling out any form. His mother said, from behind the kettle, "They mail you a card, don't they?" No card had come. He texted Ethan, who sent back a photo of his own voter information card propped against a cereal box like a trophy, and then Aurelie, who replied only: "just go. it's canada, not a moon colony."

The polling place was the community hall on Fairview Road, the same low brick building where he'd taken bad piano recitals and where, two Sundays ago, relatives had stood up one after another to eulogize his grandmother until the room smelled of carnations and old perfume. That was the trouble with the hall: it kept doubling. He couldn't walk into it without both versions happening at once, grief and folding chairs, and now a third version, democracy, waiting to be added.

Aurelie was already on the steps, eating sunflower seeds out of her jacket pocket and spitting the shells into the flowerbed with an ease that suggested she'd done it through several elections. Inside the double doors, a line threaded between the bake-sale tables, which still bore faint rings from coffee cups; the air held floor wax and something sweet from the kitchen, lemon loaf maybe. He told her his worry quietly, as if admitting to a missing homework assignment. "What if I'm not on the list? What if I missed my one chance and have to wait four years?"

She cracked another shell between her teeth. "Do you actually know that, or are you just panicking in a reasonable-sounding voice?"

It was a fair distinction, and it stopped him. He had, in Ms. Luo's philosophy class last semester, spent a genuinely embarrassing amount of one evening reading about epistemology, the study of how we know what we claim to know, mostly because the word had looked impressive in a textbook margin. He had never expected it to be useful. But standing in the wax-smelling hallway, he noticed he was treating an assumption as a fact, and the noticing itself felt like a small tool sliding into his hand. He didn't know that unregistered voters were turned away. He only feared it.

The line moved faster than the line at the funeral, which had gone out the doors and down the ramp, old neighbours in black standing patient in April wind. At the table, a woman with reading glasses on a beaded chain asked for his card. He said he didn't have one, braced for the booth of last resort, whatever that would be. She didn't sigh or frown. She said, "Then you can register right here today," and pulled a sheet toward him, and asked for proof of identity and address, and his hands were steadier than he expected as he laid down his driver's licence and a bank statement he'd grabbed on the way out, mostly on Aurelie's advice.

"You can just do that?" he asked, filling in his name. "Register on election day, at the polling place?"

"Every election," she said, already looking past him to the next voter. "It says so right on the form."

Behind him, Ethan arrived breathless and collar-dented, having sprinted from the bus stop, and watched over Alexander's shoulder as the pen moved. "Wait," Ethan said. "I've been panicking about my card all week. I thought you needed it. I was going to go home."

"You can register here too," Alexander said. "Same desk. It takes a pen." It occurred to him that his panic and Ethan's panic had been identical and equally useless, two people guarding a rule that didn't exist, and that Aurelie, who had never read a page of philosophy in her life, had simply known the difference between a fear and a fact. There was more than one way to hold knowledge, apparently. Some of it came from textbooks in margins, and some of it came from being the kind of person who says "do you actually know that?" out loud.

The ballot itself was anticlimactic, a strip of card behind a cardboard screen, a pencil on a string. He stood there longer than he meant to. He had read the platforms twice, argued them at lunch until Ms. Luo, walking past their table, had said only, "Uncertainty honestly held is worth more than certainty borrowed," and kept walking, and he'd thought at the time it was a bit much. Now, pencil hovering, he understood it as permission. There were things he was sure of and things he wasn't, and the mark he made could live with both.

He folded the ballot, slid it into the box, and heard the soft wooden clack of it landing among the others. On his way out, the bake-sale table was doing a modest trade, and an older man was arguing cheerfully with the cashier about the price of lemon loaf, saying he wasn't indigent, he was thrifty, and the cashier laughed and gave him the slice anyway. Aurelie was waiting on the steps with the last of her sunflower seeds. "Well?" she said. "Feel different?" He thought about it honestly, and said, "Ask me in four years," and held the door for an old woman coming in slow, cane first, her voter card held out in front of her like a ticket to something.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In periodized training, a season is divided into cycles; a microcycle, the smallest, usually lasts about one week.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and cold metal, and Laurence had the clipboard balanced on her knees because the bleachers were the only place to sit. On the clipboard was a week, seven empty boxes, and above the boxes a title she had crossed out twice: Training Plan, then My Plan, then nothing. She was trying to fill Monday through Sunday with runs, and every version she drafted filled all seven days, because seven days of running felt like seriousness and six felt like a confession.

Arianne dropped onto the bench below her, unwrapping a protein bar with her teeth. "You're still doing that?"

"Ms. Shin wants it Friday." Laurence tapped the pen against Monday. "Ten kilometers. Tuesday ten. Wednesday I was thinking twelve, because Wednesday's nothing else."

"That's not a plan, that's a list of ways to hurt yourself."

"It's a plan. It has numbers."

Arianne pointed the half-eaten bar at the page. "Where's the rest?"

"There isn't one. Rest is for people who have time to rest."

Arianne said nothing to that, which was worse than arguing, and Laurence wrote 12 in Wednesday's box anyway, pressing hard enough to tear the paper a little. She knew what Arianne was doing, withholding agreement like it was a currency, and she hated that it worked. She'd been the one who decided, back in September, that she would train like the girls who placed at regionals trained, and if that meant being a small autocrat over her own body, issuing decrees about pace and distance, then fine. She'd read enough quotes taped inside lockers to know that discipline was supposed to underwrite everything else. Ambition, presumably. College recruiting letters, maybe, though no letter had come yet and the season was half over.

At the far end of the gym Hubert was supposed to be setting up volleyball standards, but he'd stopped to read the practice schedule taped to the wall, one hand still on a pole. He called over without turning around. "Laurence, is yours the thing with the boxes? Shin showed me one from last year. She keeps them."

"Why would she keep them?"

"To prove you planned rest. She rejected Fenwick's whole program last spring. No rest days. Made him redo it in a night."

Laurence looked at her seven filled boxes. Her Thursday said 10 easy, which was her idea of a concession, a pace so slow it barely counted as running but still counted as running. She wrote it smaller than the others, hoping it would look like a placeholder.

She found Ms. Shin in the equipment room, counting cones onto a cart. Ms. Shin did not look up when Laurence held out the clipboard, but she stopped counting, which meant she was reading.

"Where's the warm-up?" Ms. Shin said.

"Stretching. Before."

"Written where?"

Laurence took the clipboard back. In the doorway she stood a moment, and because Ms. Shin was already counting again, cones falling into the cart like a slow clock, she asked the question in the flattest voice she could manage, to make it sound technical instead of desperate. "How do you split a season? Is there a way?"

"Talk to Hubert," Ms. Shin said. "He's been reading the coaching manual since he broke his wrist. He thinks it makes him a coach."

Hubert was sitting on a rolled mat now, wrist brace on one arm, and when Laurence sat down across from him he pulled a battered binder out of his bag like he'd been waiting all week for someone to ask. He turned pages of other people's fluorescent highlighter. "Okay, so the whole season gets divided into cycles," he said. "Blocks. And the smallest one is about a week." He tapped a section heading. "Coaches call it a microcycle."

"That's just a week with a fancy name."

"That's a week with a shape," Hubert said. "Hard days, easy days, a rest day, arranged so they add up to something instead of just piling up."

Laurence took the binder and read the highlighted lines herself, twice. She had wanted a formula and instead there was a way of thinking, which was more work. She thought of her September self, decreeing ten kilometers a day like rest was a tax on the weak, and she thought of Arianne's silence, which had never actually been empty. Maybe Arianne wasn't being generous with her doubt, wasn't being altruistic about it at all; maybe she just thought Laurence was wrong and was too decent to spend the argument. Laurence couldn't decide which was true and suspected it didn't matter. Both could be.

She borrowed Hubert's pen and rebuilt the week on the back page. Monday hard, Tuesday easy, Wednesday hard, Thursday easy plus drills, Friday nothing at all, a whole box that said rest in letters bigger than any distance. She wrote warm-ups into every day, dynamic before, stretching after, each in its own small column, until the plan looked less like a decree and more like something that could survive contact with her actual life. Saturday hard, Sunday easy. One microcycle, arranged. She could admit she didn't yet know whether the arrangement was right, only that it had a shape now, and that she'd find out in her legs the following week.

Friday morning she handed the clipboard to Ms. Shin outside the equipment room, and Ms. Shin read it through once, nodded, and said, "Good. Now do the whole season. Forty of these. Due in two weeks."

Hubert, passing with a cart of volleyballs, grinned at her expression.

"Want the binder back?" he said.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result.
story:
Maria's mother had printed the interview tips from the restaurant's website and left them on the kitchen table beside a bus schedule. At the bottom, under a heading about answering questions, the page said: "We recommend the STAR method." Maria read the line twice, then folded the sheet into her back pocket and texted Dave.

Dave was already at the library when she arrived, sitting with three empty cups from the vending machine and his chemistry notes pushed to one side. "I have an interview Saturday," Maria said. "At Il Forno. There's this thing called the STAR method and I don't know what it is."

"Sounds like a missile defense system," Dave said.

"It says it answers interview questions about past behavior." She flattened the page on the table between them. "That's all it says. Then it goes straight into dress codes."

Boston slid into the seat across from them, late, holding a bag of chips he had clearly bought on the walk over. He read the page upside down. "Past behavior. So they ask you about something you did, and you have to have done something."

"That is not helpful," Maria said. But the phrase stayed with her on the bus home. Questions about past behavior. Not hypotheticals, not what would you do if, but what had she actually done. She thought about the group project in tenth grade, the one that had gone wrong. Ms. Owusu had assigned it in October, four people, one grade, and by the second week two of them had stopped answering messages. Maria had ended up assembling the whole presentation at midnight, angry, and it had gone fine, which somehow made her angrier. She had never told anyone the shape of that month.

On Friday she tried to tell it to Dave in the school parking lot, as practice. "So the project was a disaster," she began. "We got an A anyway, but only because I did everything."

Dave shook his head. "You started with the ending. You told me the result first, and then the middle, and I still don't know what the project was."

"It was a documentary about water rights."

"See, I didn't even know that. Start over."

She started over twice more and both times it came out tangled, all out of order, the A first, then a complaint, then a detail about a broken microphone that belonged nowhere. Boston, leaning against the fence, said, "You're telling it like it's a pile. It needs a shape." Then he paused, took out his phone, and looked something up. "Here. STAR. It's on job sites everywhere. It means you describe the Situation, then the Task, the Action you took, and the Result. In that order."

Maria made him say it again while she wrote it on her hand, because the printout at home had cut off before the definition, or else she had never scrolled far enough. Situation, Task, Action, Result. It was almost insultingly simple, and yet when she tried it in the car while her mother drove, the story of the water rights project finally had a spine. The situation: four people, one documentary, a deadline in three weeks. The task: get it finished at a passing standard. The action: she had divided what remained into parts, sent each person a specific piece with a specific deadline, and done the filming herself when no one responded. The result: the documentary screened on time, the two silent members showed up for the presentation, and the group got an A. Told that way, it sounded less like a grievance and more like something she had managed. She wasn't sure the A was the real result. The real result might have been that she had learned she could finish something alone and had hated finishing it alone. She kept both versions in her head and did not decide between them.

At Il Forno on Saturday, the manager, a broad man with a pen behind his ear, sat her at a corner table and asked the questions she had expected: availability, weekends, whether she had ever handled food. Then he said, "Tell me about a time you had a conflict with someone on a team and how you handled it."

"Last year," Maria said, "I was in a group of four making a documentary, and two of the members stopped communicating." She kept going in order. The situation, then the task, then what she had done, and finally the result, and she watched the manager's pen move across his clipboard at the point where she described splitting the remaining work. When she finished, he nodded once.

"You'd be surprised how many people answer that question with a theory," he said. "You actually answered it." He asked her about the register, about whether she could carry four plates, and then he stood and shook her hand. He said she could start the following Saturday, subject to a food handler's certificate, which the restaurant would underwrite the cost of as long as she stayed ninety days.

She walked out past the patio tables where Ms. Owusu sat with a coffee and a crossword, one of the restaurant's few Saturday regulars. Ms. Owusu waved her over. "Well? How was it?"

"I got it, I think. He said I could start next week."

"Doing what you did in my class, I hope, and not what those two boys did." Ms. Owusu had never resolved the dispute over who had contributed what; she had refused to act as an arbitration panel and simply graded the documentary as a whole. At the time Maria had thought that was unfair. Now, holding a job offer she had earned partly by narrating that same project, she thought the fairness of the grade and the truth of the work were two different things, and she said so.

Ms. Owusu looked at her over the crossword. "Growing up," she said, "sounds bellicose when you put it that way."

"It wasn't a fight," Maria said. "It was more like accounting."

Ms. Owusu laughed and folded the paper. "Go home and tell your mother. And Maria, when the Saturday rush comes and a table sends back a plate, remember that nobody in that kitchen cares about your situation, your task, or your result."

Maria put her hand, with the four words still inked across it, back in her pocket, and walked to the bus stop.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Blocking is the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals.
story:
The actors collided at the top of scene two, again, and Aaron watched from the fourth row with his clipboard held against his chest like a shield.

"You were both downstage left," he said. "Simran, you crossed during Martin's line. Martin, you crossed during Simran's line. Physically, mathematically, there was nowhere else for you to go."

Martin rubbed his shoulder with theatrical dignity. "I was following my instinct."

"Your instinct has a concussion," said Simran.

Aaron had been handed the one-act by Ms. Sinclair, who ran the community theatre's summer program and had a policy of giving the directors under nineteen something they could fail at safely. He had assumed directing meant having opinions about the lines. It had not occurred to him, until Tuesday's rehearsal, that it also meant deciding where every human body stood and moved for forty continuous minutes, and that if he did not decide, the bodies would decide for themselves, badly.

He stayed after everyone left and walked the empty stage with the script under his arm, stepping through scene two alone. He moved to the window, crossed to the table, sat, stood. The plywood floor creaked under him like something complaining. He pencilled a small arrow in the margin and then, feeling both ridiculous and official, wrote a note to himself: Martin crosses first, on "weather," Simran holds. It was the first time the whole evening had felt like his.

At home he found a message from Ms. Sinclair, printed on yellow paper and left in his mailbox, because she believed text messages were for people with no patience.

Aaron, she wrote. I hear there was a pileup in scene two. When I was nineteen I put two actors in the same chair for an entire Chekhov play, which on a steppe set at least looked intentional. Here is the only advice I will give you, and you may ignore it: the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage is set by the director during rehearsals. There is a word for it. Ask Martin's mother, she was an actress. Do not ask me again. Bring tape Thursday.

Martin's mother turned out to be a small, pugnacious woman who attended rehearsals in a folding chair near the back like a retired general observing field exercises. Aaron approached her during the break, holding two plastic cups of lemonade he did not want.

"Ms. Sinclair said there's a word for all this," he said. "The positions, the moves."

"Blocking," she said, not looking up from her crossword. "Everything on that stage is blocked, or it's an accident. Mostly at your age it's accidents." She took one of the lemonades.

He went home and blocked the entire play that night on graph paper, drawing the furniture to scale, plotting every crossing with a ruler. He had started the summer believing that structure was the enemy of feeling, that real performance was spontaneous or it was nothing. The graph paper argued otherwise. It occurred to him, somewhere around midnight, ruler in hand, that the positions might be planned precisely so that the feelings could be reckless, that a fixed floor was what made flight possible. He did not fully believe this yet. But he pencilled it in the margin anyway, next to the arrow.

Thursday he brought blue painter's tape and laid down marks for every entrance, every chair, every window. Martin walked his crosses and found that when he no longer had to worry about being hit, he actually listened to Simran's lines for the first time, and answered them differently, softer. Simran stopped glancing sideways before every move. The scene ran clean twice in a row, and the second time nobody noticed it had run clean, which Aaron understood was the point.

Martin stayed after to help pull up the tape. "I owe you an apology," he said, peeling a long blue strip with great care, as though it were a bandage. "I thought you were being a control freak. But knowing where I'm going is the only reason I can do anything interesting on the way."

"You can be both," Aaron said. "A control freak and right."

On Friday Ms. Sinclair sat in the back row and watched the run-through without expression, arms folded, and afterward she said only, "Scene two," and let it hang there until Aaron's stomach had fully dropped, and then she said, "Don't touch it," and left.

Saturday night, before the house opened, Aaron stood in the wings watching the audience come in, ordinary people settling into folding seats, and he thought about how they would never see the graph paper or the tape or the pencilled arrows, how all his deciding would look, from out there, like people simply choosing to stand where they stood. There was a version of directing that was invisible, and a version that was furniture, and he had no idea yet which one he was doing, or whether they were different things at all. Simran bumped his shoulder on her way to the stage and said, "Places, genius," and he picked up his clipboard and followed the blue marks into the dark.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Ontario high school students must complete 40 hours of community involvement to earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma.
story:
The deadline lived on the refrigerator, where her mother had taped it in October: forms due to the guidance office by the last Friday of May. Brooklyn read it while she ate her cereal, then again while she rinsed the bowl, the way you reread something hoping the number will have shrunk. Eleven hours. After two years of promising herself she would get to it, she had eleven hours of community involvement logged, and Ontario was not going to hand her a diploma without forty. That was the whole arrangement, no appeals, no exceptions she'd ever heard of. She pulled on her boots and texted Dion on the way out.

The food bank occupied the basement of a church two streets from her house, close enough that she'd walked past it a thousand times without once going in. Amari had told her it took walk-in volunteers on Saturdays, which was how the three of them ended up at nine in the morning in a room that smelled of cardboard and disinfectant, facing a wall of shelves marked in Mr. Chanthavong's tidy handwriting: PASTA, CANNED FRUIT, BABY, MISC.

"You're the ones chasing hours," Mr. Chanthavong said. He was the neighbour from four doors down, the one whose lawn she'd admired all her life without knowing his name until Amari introduced them. "Grade twelves always come in May. We're glad, don't misunderstand. But I'll tell you what I tell everyone: the work doesn't care why you came."

He put them on the sorting table. Dion dated cans; Amari weighed rice into bags; Brooklyn entered inventory into a laptop so old the space bar stuck. It was slower work than she'd expected, and quieter, and she found she liked the rhythm of it, the small verdict of each can: keep, discard, keep.

At lunch Amari leaned against the shelving with her sandwich. "My cousin waited too," she said. "She ended up stacking chairs at a funeral home for the last six hours. At least you got pasta." Brooklyn laughed, but something in her kept turning the morning over. She'd walked in believing the forty hours were a toll, a gate she had to pass through to get where she was actually going, and she'd spent months resenting it with a resentment that had hardened into something almost intransigent, a certainty that forced service was a contradiction in terms. Real volunteering, she'd argued in a class debate last fall, had to be freely chosen or it wasn't volunteering at all. Dion had taken the other side that day, and she remembered it now, the two of them at the back of Mr. Chanthavong's church basement eating donated granola bars.

"You're thinking too loud," Dion said.

"I'm revising an opinion. Give me a minute." She told them about the debate, how she'd been so sure. But the morning had muddied it, and she was honest enough to admit that motive might be a confounder rather than the whole experiment: whether she'd come for the hours or for the pasta, the pasta was sorted either way, and a family she'd never meet would cook it tonight. Maybe the requirement hadn't ruined the good of the act. Maybe it had catalyzed it, started something that wouldn't have started on its own, and whether that made the good smaller or just different was a question she couldn't settle between bites.

When they went back in, Mr. Chanthavong signed her form without ceremony. "Nine to three," he said, showing her the line. "That's six. You'll want five more before the last Friday of May, so you'll be back, and next time you'll know where the rice goes."

Outside, the evening was still bright. Amari and Dion walked ahead arguing about whether funeral homes counted as food banks for the purposes of the diploma, and Brooklyn lagged behind them, holding the signed form flat against her binder so the ink wouldn't smudge, the way you carry something that is only paper and is also, somehow, the whole spring.

"Brooklyn," Dion called over his shoulder. "You coming or not?"

She jogged to catch up, form still pressed to her chest.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A 1985 study by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky called basketball's 'hot hand' an illusion, but a 2018 reanalysis by Miller and Sanjurjo found a statistical flaw and evidence of streak shooting.
story:
The Hendersons' den smelled like nacho cheese and wet umbrellas, because it had started raining halfway through the second quarter and everybody had crowded inside. Payton sat on the arm of the couch with her plate balanced on her knee, watching number 23 drain his fourth three in a row. The whole room came up off the cushions. Her father, who had lived next door to the Hendersons for eleven years and treated their den like his own, kept shouting the same word: hot, hot, hot.

"He is on fire," Justin said from the floor, gesturing at the screen with a tortilla chip. "Nobody can tell me that's random. He's made four straight."

"It's five now," Jewel said, and the room roared again before anyone could argue, because number 23 had just done it again from the corner.

"You know that's an illusion, right?" Payton said it quieter than she meant to, into the gap between possessions, and half the room turned. Her ears went hot. She had read about it two weeks ago, down a rabbit hole at midnight when she should have been asleep, and she'd been waiting, a little shamefully, for exactly this moment. "There was this study in 1985. Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky. They called it the hot hand, and they called it an illusion."

"Who are those people," her father said, not really a question, the way he said it when he planned to keep believing whatever he already believed.

"Researchers," Payton said. "They looked at shooting data and said streaks don't mean anything. Every shot's basically independent."

Jewel passed the salsa down the line of hands without being asked, because Mr. Henderson had that look of wanting it and being too polite to interrupt. Payton watched her do it and felt, briefly, like a worse person, the kind who expropriates a room's good mood for the sake of being right. She hadn't come here to take anything from anybody. She just wanted somebody to check her math.

"Then explain tonight," Justin said, sweeping his chip at the screen. "Five straight."

"Okay, but here's the thing." Payton set her plate down. "In 2018, Miller and Sanjurjo reanalyzed it. They found a statistical flaw in the original study." She paused, because this was the part she still turned over at night, the encapsulation of the whole argument in one sentence that somehow made it both clearer and stranger. "And they found evidence of streak shooting. Actual streaks. So the hot hand might be real after all."

"Wait." Justin's eyebrows went up. "So which is it?"

"That's what I'm saying. That's the whole problem."

Ms. Brown, the Hendersons' neighbor from across the cul-de-sac, who had come over for the halftime cobbler and stayed for the yelling, leaned forward in the recliner. "So the first study says the player's not really hot. The second one says, hold on, maybe he is."

"Basically," Payton said. "One found a flaw in the other."

Her father snorted, but kindly. "So science took thirty-three years to agree with me."

"It didn't agree with you, Dad. It found a flaw." She was careful with it, careful the way she'd learned to be when the two of them argued, because he wasn't really arguing about basketball. He was arguing that a person could feel something true in his chest, and she was arguing that a feeling needed a spreadsheet, and they'd been having some version of this fight since she'd stopped just agreeing with him at dinner. Tonight she wasn't sure the spreadsheet won. That was the part she couldn't get right in her own head. If the 2018 paper said streak shooting was real, then her father's certainty had been right for the wrong reasons, which was somehow more annoying than him being wrong.

The game came back from timeout and everybody's attention splintered, but Justin stayed turned around on the floor, elbows on the couch cushion. "So if it's real now, then what was the flaw?"

"I don't fully get the flaw," Payton admitted. "Something in how they counted. That's honestly as far as I got."

"Huh," Justin said, and he said it like it was the most interesting thing anyone had said all night, which made her feel seen in a way she hadn't expected and didn't entirely trust.

Number 23 got the ball in transition, wide open at the top of the key. The room rose as one, and Payton rose with them, and she realized she wanted him to make it. Six straight. Whatever the data said, she wanted it, wanted it with a hedonistic, unscientific joy she had no intention of apologizing for. The shot went up, hung on the rim, and dropped through.

Her father didn't say I told you so. He just put his hand briefly on top of her head, the way he used to when she was small, and Ms. Brown pressed the last of the cobbler into Jewel's hands because Jewel had missed it the first time around.

"So the hot hand's real," Justin said, "but you can't prove it to the guy sitting next to you."

"I can't prove anything," Payton said. "I can just tell you who studied it and when. The rest is tonight."

On the screen, number 23 held his follow-through, three fingers still raised at the ceiling, and the whole den held its breath for the next one.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A pyramid with a wide base and narrow top shows a high birth rate and a young population, pointing to a growing need for schools and teachers.
story:
The flyer had been taped to the door of the geography room since September, curling at the corners: two weeks building classrooms in one of two partner countries, and every applicant had to submit a page arguing which site needed the school more. Chase had ignored it until the last week of applications, when Karina sat down across from him in the library and slid her finished page across the table.

"Hers is better already," Brooklynn said from the next seat, not looking up from her laptop. Brooklynn had spent a month of lunch periods on hers, and she wanted the trip badly enough that she had stopped lending Chase her notes in chemistry. He was fairly sure that was about the trip too, since only one student from each school went.

Chase needed the trip for his own reasons, which he had not said out loud to anyone: his father was home that autumn, convalescing after a surgery that had gone from routine to serious in the space of a phone call, and the apartment had developed a malaise that Chase could not name but could feel the moment he opened the door, the television murmuring, the curtains half drawn even at noon. Two weeks away had begun to look less like volunteering and more like breathing.

Ms. Ba had given them one hint before closing her door for the afternoon: look at the population pyramids, she said, they tell you everything. Chase found them that evening at the library, two bar charts turned sideways, ages stacked up the side and population spread out along the bottom. He stared for twenty minutes and understood nothing. One country's chart looked like an actual pyramid; the other looked like a barrel, thick in the middle, hardly wider at the bottom than the top. He almost closed the laptop.

"Wait," Karina said, leaning over from her side of the table. She pointed at the pyramid-shaped one. "Look where the people are. They're all at the bottom. The bottom is the young part." She traced the wide base with her finger. "So that's a high birth rate, and a young population." Chase wrote it down and then stopped, because Karina had already turned back to her own page, and he did not want her to see that she had handed him the whole thing.

But she hadn't, not quite. Sitting with it alone, at home, with his father asleep down the hall, Chase found the part that was his. The barrel-shaped country, aging and slow-growing, was building nursing homes and hiring caregivers; he had read that in an article he could now actually understand, because he could see it in the shape. "A wide base and a narrow top," he said quietly, testing it, "shows a high birth rate and a young population, pointing to a growing need for schools and teachers." The pyramid country needed the classrooms. The barrel country needed something else entirely. What he could not figure out, and was honest enough to write, was whether two weeks of unskilled seventeen-year-old labor met either need, or whether the trip was mostly for the volunteers.

He submitted it that way, question included. In the interview the next week, Ms. Ba read the page twice and did not smile, exactly, but she tapped the final paragraph. "Most students hide the part they don't know," she said. "You put it in the conclusion." She told him he was going to the pyramid country, and that Brooklynn, who had written a smoother page with no questions in it, would go to the other site, the one building the nursing home annex. Brooklynn did not speak to him for three days.

On the last afternoon before the trip, Chase stopped at his father's door. The curtains were open for once, a small correction his father had made on his own, and the light lay across the blanket in a long pale stripe. "Two weeks," Chase said. "There's food in the freezer, and Karina's mom said she'd check in." His father looked at him for a moment and then said, "Take the good flashlight, the one in the hall closet," which was the closest he came, those months, to saying anything about leaving or staying. Chase got the flashlight, and the new notebooks Ms. Ba had bought for the whole group, and stood outside the school at dusk waiting for the van, watching the lit windows of the geography room go dark one floor at a time.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In translation, the ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins amino acids together with peptide bonds to build a protein chain.
story:
The kitchen table had been cleared of everything except her notebook, a bag of pony beads she'd found in the junk drawer, and a ball of twine. Samantha bent a paperclip into a hook and tried to thread a blue bead onto the string. Behind her, Kenzie let herself in through the back door without knocking, the way she always did.

"You're doing the craft thing again," Kenzie said. She dropped her bag on a chair. "The exam's in fourteen hours."

"That's why I'm doing the craft thing." Samantha held up the string. A row of beads sat on it, green, yellow, yellow, red. "I failed the first attempt because I memorized the words and couldn't say what any of them were doing. Ms. Lin wrote one thing on my paper. She wrote, tell it back like a story. So I'm telling it back."

Kenzie sat down, unconvinced, and picked up a bead to roll between her fingers. Logan arrived ten minutes later, hair damp from the walk, and stood in the doorway with the expression of someone who had already passed the unit test and found the whole enterprise faintly lugubrious. He pulled out a chair anyway.

"Look," he said, "transcription is easy, RNA polymerase makes the mRNA copy, whatever. Translation is where you died. Just drill the words."

"That's what I did last time." Samantha laid the string flat and pointed to the beads. "Translation is this. The mRNA is the string with the pattern on it, and the ribosome is me, moving along it, reading the pattern, picking up the right bead for each spot." She slid her fingers forward along the twine, matching each bead to a scribbled code in her notebook. "Each bead is an amino acid. And the ribosome joins them together with peptide bonds." She said the last part to the beads as much as to them. "That's how you build a protein chain."

"So it's like threading beads while you read the pattern," Kenzie said slowly.

"Exactly like that. Except you're also gluing them as you go, so it comes out one chain." Samantha pulled the string taut so the beads pressed together. "One chain, and that chain is the protein."

Logan had picked up her notebook without asking. He read for a while, his mouth slightly open, and she watched him go from polite to absorbed. "I always pictured the amino acids floating in and getting assembled somewhere," he admitted. "I never pictured anything moving along anything."

"Neither did I. That's what Ms. Lin's note meant, I think. The words are just words until you can see somebody's hands doing something." She hesitated, because she didn't want to concede it too easily. "You were right that I have to drill too. I can understand the picture and still blank on the vocabulary tomorrow. It's both."

They drilled for an hour. Kenzie quizzed her on the codon chart, then quizzed her again, harder, arguing about a disputed answer until Samantha found the table in the textbook and had to adjudicate between them. Kenzie was wrong about the stop codon and took it badly for about ninety seconds, then wrote it on her wrist in pen. Logan, who had started the evening saying he only came by to eat their snacks, ended up narrating the whole process back to Samantha twice, walking his fingers along the twine, saying peptide bonds with the satisfaction of someone who has discovered that a word has a shape.

At eleven her mother came down in her robe, looked at the table covered in beads and torn notebook pages, and decided against asking. She put water on for tea and went back upstairs.

Samanza didn't notice. She was on her feet, string in hand, walking Kenzie through it one more time. "The ribosome moves along the messenger RNA," she said, sliding her grip forward inch by inch, "and it joins the amino acids together as it goes." She reached the end of the string and lifted the finished chain above the table, beads clicking against each other.

"Finished protein," Kenzie said.

"Finished protein." Samantha set it down carefully, then wound the twine around her wrist like a bracelet. She would wear it into the exam room if Ms. Lin allowed it, and if not, she would remember her own hands moving. "Same time before the next test?"

Logan was already threading a second string, frowning at the code table. "This one's mine," he said.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In transcription, the enzyme RNA polymerase reads one strand of DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA, which carries the gene's instructions.
story:
Isaac's cousin Danny sat at the kitchen table turning a glass of milk in slow circles, waiting for the game they'd been promised, and Isaac laid out the index cards he'd been avoiding for a week. The cards were Izabella's, borrowed on Friday, her neat handwriting covering both sides. Izabella had also, in the parking lot, in a voice quieter than usual, told him what Ms. Farah had said in the staff room, and Isaac had thanked her and walked to his truck and sat there for a while before starting it. That part he had not told Danny.

"You said there'd be a game," Danny said. He was eleven, up from the farm for the weekend because his mother thought Isaac could keep him busy, and so far Isaac had fed him cereal and let him watch the older boy across the street wash a boat that hadn't been in water for years.

"There is a game. It's called teach it or lose it. I explain something, and you tell me if it makes sense. If it doesn't, I lose." Isaac shuffled the cards even though they were numbered, because his hands wanted something to do. "You know what DNA is."

"Coils. In you. Dad keeps semen in the freezer, it's got, like, the codes for the cows."

"Right, close enough." Isaac set down the first card. "It's a code. It's the instruction book for building a whole animal, or a person. Every cell has it. And here's the thing I have to get straight by tomorrow. The book never leaves the library."

Danny squinted at him over the milk.

"Think about the farm," Isaac said. "Your dad has one book that tells you how to mix feed for the barn. You wouldn't rip the pages out and carry them through the mud and give them to the pigs. You'd copy down what you need and take the copy."

"Because the book would get wrecked."

"Because the book would get wrecked, and there's only one of it. So the cell does the same thing. The DNA stays where it is. When the cell needs to build something, it makes a working copy." He tapped the card, though Danny couldn't read Izabella's cramped loops from across the table. "There's an enzyme. It's called RNA polymerase."

"Enzyme like in the stomach?"

"Like that, yeah, a thing that does a job. The RNA polymerase reads one strand of the DNA." He uncoiled a bit of thread from his sleeve, the blue thread from his jacket cuff that had been hanging loose all morning, and laid it straight on the table between the salt and Danny's milk. "Just this one strand, like reading one line of the page. And as it reads, it builds a matching strand. A copy. The copy is called messenger RNA, and it carries the gene's instructions out into the cell, where they get read and turned into protein. That's the whole idea. The original stays safe, the copy does the work."

Danny looked at the thread. "So the cows are made out of copies."

"Everything is made out of copies. Your hair. Milk." Isaac rolled the thread back up and put it in his pocket, and that was when he heard his father's truck in the driveway, earlier than it should have been. His father had been on furlough from the plant since March, home Tuesdays and Thursdays and lately most Fridays too, and on the days he was home he moved through the kitchen like a man checking whether the house was still standing.

His father came in with a paper sack of groceries, nodded at Danny, looked at the index cards spread across the table where the placemats should have been. "Study session?"

"Helping Danny with his homework," Isaac said. It came out too fast, and his father's eyes stayed on him a second longer than the sentence deserved. Danny, thank God, was drinking his milk.

His father put away the bread, the off-brand cereal, the eggs. At the doorway he paused. "Ms. Farah called the house yesterday. I wasn't home. Your mother took it." Then he went down the hall, and Isaac heard the bedroom door, not slammed, just closed.

Danny watched him with the frankness of an eleven-year-old. "You're in trouble."

"I'm not in trouble." The exam was Monday morning, seven forty, in Ms. Farah's room, the retake she'd granted him after what she'd found on his first attempt, the phone she'd set face-down on her desk without a word while the room went silent around him. He hadn't told his father any of it. He'd told Izabella he'd rather handle it himself, and she'd looked at him the way she looked at lab partners who said they'd already cleaned the beakers. "I have to know this stuff by tomorrow, that's all. So I need you to tell me the parts that don't make sense."

"The messenger part," Danny said. "Why's it called a messenger?"

"Because it carries the instructions to where they're used. Like a guy on a bike delivering the copied recipe to the barn." Isaac gathered the cards, squared them, and dealt them out between them like a hand of poker. "Okay. You ask, I answer. And if I get one wrong, you get the last piece of pie."

"Deal," Danny said, and slid his milk aside to make room.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The area between two curves is found by integrating the upper function minus the lower function over the interval where they are ordered that way.
story:
The corner store on Marsh Street smelled of floor wax and the oranges Mr. García kept in a wooden crate by the register, and Nicholas had come there for a cherry cola and a place to spread out his homework, because his house that week held only his father's silence and the boxes for the move. He set his binder on the counter by the coffee machine, and Mr. García, who had watched Nicholas grow taller over four years of after-school purchases, slid him a stool without being asked.

"Justina says I'm wrong," said June, arriving with her own binder already open, her biology textbook wedged under one arm. "We got different areas for the same problem, so one of us is wrong, and she says it's me." She laid her notebook on the counter beside his, and there they were: two neat solutions to the same problem, a line and a parabola, an interval from one crossing point to the other, and two different numbers circled at the bottom. Justina came in behind her, dropping coins on the counter for a bag of salted almonds, still holding her pencil like a weapon.

The problem had come from math club the day before, which Nicholas had attended for the first time in months. Flashback pressed in on him as he looked at the two solutions: the club met in Mr. García's old classroom before Mr. García retired and bought the store, the desks pushed into a rough circle, the seniors at the far table whom everyone seemed to lionize, their shirts from the state competition, their calculators holstered like sidearms. Nicholas had sat near the window with the juniors and said almost nothing, but he had copied the problem down, and he had watched Justina and June argue about it even then, the argument following them out into the hallway and apparently all the way to tonight.

They showed him the work on the counter, right there between the lottery machine and the rack of motor oil. Justina had set up her integral one way and June the other, June subtracting the line's expression from the parabola's, Justina subtracting the parabola's from the line's, and each of them integrating carefully, each of them checking twice, and the two answers disagreeing completely. June had even divided her answer in half to see if that reconciled anything, and it hadn't, and she had started to suspect the textbook itself.

"You have to subtract one from the other," Justina said. "Which one, that's the whole fight."

Nicholas drank some of the cola and drew the two curves on his own paper, quick sketch, the line rising steeply, the parabola opening upward and flatter, crossing the line twice, the region between them closed like a lens. He shaded it lightly. June leaned over his shoulder, and her biology homework slipped partway out of her textbook, a worksheet about river ecosystems, the word riparian highlighted twice in the margin, zones of green along a streambank, and for a moment he thought about the shaded lens he had drawn as its own small territory, bounded by its two curves the way the riparian strip was bounded by the water and the dry hills, everything that mattered living in between.

"The area between them," he said slowly, not looking up. "It's the same shape no matter how you describe it. So the subtraction has to come out the same, positive either way." He tapped the sketch. "The upper one minus the lower one. You integrate the upper function minus the lower function, over the part of the interval where they're ordered that way." He pointed at the space between the crossings, where the line sat above the parabola everywhere, no switching, no argument about which was which. "If you subtract them the other way around, you're just getting the negative of the area. Area underneath, not area."

June flipped back through her work, her finger running down the page, and stopped at her setup, and her face changed. "I had it upside down," she said. "I subtracted the lower from the upper. I mean the upper from the lower. Mine's negative hers, exactly, look." Justina compared them and nodded, and neither of them said anything for a second, and then June laughed, one short exhale, the kind that lets go of an entire afternoon. "I did the calculus right and the subtraction backwards. That's the worst possible combination."

"Take the whole interval," Justina said, still checking. "The line stays above the parabola the whole way between the crossings. That's why it worked out so cleanly."

"That's the only reason it worked out," Nicholas said, and here he slowed down, because something was bothering him and he decided to say it anyway. "If the curves crossed in the middle, you couldn't just pick one order for everything. You'd have to split the interval where they switch, upper minus lower in each piece." He looked at his sketch, at the two clean crossings, at the lens of shaded pencil between them. "We haven't done a problem like that, so I'm guessing. But it seems like it has to be true."

Mr. García, who had been restocking the cigarette shelf and pretending not to listen, came over and put three more oranges in the crate without a word about any of it. He looked at the shaded drawing, and at the three of them leaning over the counter, and said only, "Store closes at ten." June bought her almonds after all, and Justina photographed Nicholas's sketch for the club's group chat, and outside the window the streetlight came on over the pumps of the old gas station, and Nicholas started redrawing the problem with a shifted line, one that crossed the parabola in the middle, just to see.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people.
story:
The assignment sheet said the plays would be performed Friday after school in the cafeteria, which meant Amelia had three days to write something and two rehearsals to stage it. She had spent the first evening drafting a piece about the whole summer her grandmother was sick, six scenes, from the hospital waiting room to the porch to the funeral home parking lot. She read it aloud to herself in the kitchen and it took twenty-two minutes.

In the drama room the next morning, Ms. Addo went around the circle asking for running times. When Amelia said twenty-two, Tyrone laughed into his sleeve, and Bradley, who was running the lights, said, "That's not a play, that's a mini-series."

"Try mine," Tyrone said, and read his first page, which was all stage directions, a beach, then a car, then a diner. Ms. Addo let him finish and then said only, "Count your locations."

Amelia counted hers at lunch, sitting on the floor outside the theater with her notebook open on her knees. Six locations. And eight people, counting the nurse who had one line and the aunt who cried in the corner. She was still counting when Tyrone sat down across from her with his own notebook, which had four locations, and a look on his face like he'd been mugged.

"Ten minutes," he said. "She says a ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters. Because there's no time to change scenery or introduce a lot of people." He tapped his pen against his knee. "So I have to pick one moment. Out of the whole thing. One."

"Which moment?"

"That's the problem. The beach without the diner doesn't mean anything. The diner without the beach is just two people ordering fries."

Amelia looked down at her six scenes. The one she kept skimming past was the porch, the last week of August, when her grandmother had asked her to read the town's new noise ordinance aloud because her eyes were bad, and then argued with every clause of it, and Amelia had argued back, and it had been the only hour that summer that hadn't felt like waiting for something. One setting. Two characters. She could stage it with two chairs and the porch rail the shop class had built for last year's Our Town.

She started over on a clean page. It went slowly, then quickly. The dialogue came back to her in her grandmother's exact cadences, including the part where the old woman had said the ordinance writers were trying to impugn the whole idea of a porch, that a porch was meant for talking loudly at dusk, and Amelia had said the ordinance was about fireworks, and her grandmother had said the principle mattered more than the specifics. Amelia had been seventeen then in the way she was seventeen now, which is to say she had believed the specifics mattered more, and had said so, and been told she was ductile, bending toward whoever was talking, and had not known whether it was an insult or a compliment. She still didn't. She wrote the line in and left it there, unresolved, because taking it out would have been dishonest and resolving it would have been worse.

At Thursday's rehearsal the scene ran nine minutes and forty seconds. Bradley ran the lights from a flashlight and a dimmer switch someone had taped to a music stand. Ms. Addo watched from the third row with her arms folded and said nothing until the end, and then she said, "Who's playing your grandmother?"

"You are, if you'll do it," Amelia said, because the drama teacher she'd originally asked had a conflict, and because there was no one else left who was free at four o'clock on a Friday.

Ms. Addo considered this for longer than a comfortable silence usually lasts. "I'll do it," she said. "But I want you to direct me. Don't be polite about it. If I get her wrong, tell me."

Friday afternoon the cafeteria smelled like bleach and pulled pork from the earlier fundraiser. Tyrone's play went first, and he had solved his problem in a way Amelia wouldn't have thought of: he'd set the whole thing inside the car, with the beach and the diner happening as voices on the phone, so he kept them without changing scenery. It ran ten minutes and six seconds and got a laugh in the right place. Then the lights came down, two chairs came forward, and Ms. Addo sat in one of them with her reading glasses low on her nose while Amelia stood in the wings with the script she no longer needed, listening to her own words come back to her in an older woman's voice.

When the scene ended, the grandmother won the argument about the ordinance, which was not how it had gone in life, and Amelia heard herself whisper, "She doesn't win," and Ms. Addo, still in the chair, still in the light, turned her head toward the wings and said, "Then come tell me so."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Air resistance slows real projectiles, so a thrown ball usually lands shorter than the calculation that ignores air resistance predicts.
story:
Thomas had set the launcher on the folding table at the back edge of the yard, its muzzle angled at exactly thirty degrees, because thirty degrees was what the math wanted.

The math was the easy part, and he knew it. You split the ball's velocity into a horizontal piece and a vertical piece, the way Ms. Papadopoulos had shown them in third period, drawing the two arrows on the board until the class stopped groaning. The horizontal piece stayed constant forever, in the frictionless country where physics problems lived. The vertical piece rose, slowed, stopped, fell. Two simple problems wearing one complicated costume. He could do it in his sleep; he had, in a sense, done it in his sleep, waking at five with the range formula rearranging itself behind his eyelids.

The regional competition was in two days, and the target, a plastic hoop staked into the lawn twenty meters out, kept refusing to cooperate.

"Again," said Tessa, who was standing by the hoop with the tape measure and a look of accumulating grievance. The ball sailed, described its graceful arc, and thumped into the grass a meter and a half short. She paced it off anyway, because she was the kind of person who trusted numbers more than her own eyes. "Eighteen point four. Same as the last three."

Thomas crouched by the launcher and checked the angle, the spring compression, the mass of the ball, all of it for the fourth time. Everything matched the calculation. Everything. The calculation said twenty meters, and the lawn said eighteen point four, and the gap between those two numbers was beginning to feel like an accusation.

"Maybe your arithmetic's wrong," Matthias offered from the porch steps, where he sat eating the chips he had promised to share and had not shared.

"It's not." Thomas didn't look up. "I did it three ways. Decomposed the velocity, used the range formula, had Tessa check. It's not the arithmetic."

"Then the universe is broken," Matthias said, and crunched.
