The universe was not broken, and Thomas was beginning, with a slow and reluctant certainty, to suspect what was. He sat down on the cold grass and pulled his notebook onto his knees. The vertical and horizontal components, the neat separation, the whole clean machinery of it, all of that was true in the world where nothing resisted anything. But the yard was not that world. The yard had air in it, and the air was doing something the equations hadn't accounted for. He turned the thought over without being able to close his hand around it. Something between the launch and the landing was subtracting from the flight, and the subtraction only ever went one way.

"Say it out loud," Tessa said, walking back to him. "You get that face when you're about to either figure it out or throw the notebook."

"The math assumes no air," Thomas said. "The whole thing. The horizontal velocity is constant only if nothing is pushing back on it. But something is. Always. So the real ball is slower sideways than the paper ball, the whole way, and slow sideways means it lands short."

He looked at the hoop, then at the launcher, then at the notebook, where his beautiful solution sat in blue ink, confident and wrong about the world.

"Air resistance," Tessa said. "It slows real projectiles down. That's it, isn't it?"

"That's it. Real ball, shorter than the calculation. Every time."

Matthias came down off the porch, leaving the chips, which by his standards was a measure of seriousness. "So for the competition, what, you just guess?"

"No. You can't compute it exactly, not at our level, not in two days." Thomas hated saying that. He had spent his whole school career believing that problems yielded if you were careful enough, and here was one that did not yield, that required him to stand in front of judges and admit a gap. His father had a word for that kind of admission, though his father's word was usually penance, some old family business about expiating carelessness through labor, and this was different, this was not carelessness, this was the honest boundary of what he could know. "You adjust empirically. We launch, we measure, we nudge the angle. The theory tells us the shape of the arc. The yard tells us the rest."

They worked until the light went amber and then blue. Tessa called the numbers, Matthias retrieved the balls with theatrical suffering, and Thomas entered each result in a column he titled, after some deliberation, reality. The values clustered, 18.4, 18.3, 18.5, and the consistency of the shortfall was almost comforting, a law instead of a mistake. He raised the angle by degrees and watched the range climb and then shrink again, and somewhere in the fading light the ball dropped through the hoop with a sound like a small bell.

Tessa whooped. Matthias held up both hands. Thomas wrote down the angle, 34 degrees, and then sat looking at it, because the number was right and also not right, right for tonight's air, tonight's balls, tonight's yard, and he could not say what it would be on Saturday.

"Judges are going to ask why not thirty," Tessa said. "Everyone else will do thirty."

"Then I'll tell them," Thomas said. "Thirty is what the equation says. Thirty-four is what actually lands in the hoop. Air resistance slows the real ball, so it lands shorter than the calculation predicts, and this is how much shorter, tonight, here. Saturday it might be different. I'll measure it then too."

He folded the notebook closed and picked up the last ball from the grass, its surface cool and faintly tacky with dew.

"One more," he said, and thumbed the switch.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Adolphe Thiers's History of the French Revolution, published from 1823 to 1827, praised moderate leaders such as Mirabeau and Lafayette and condemned radicals such as Robespierre.
story:
The museum closed at five, and Jordan had until then to fill his notebook with something he could turn into an essay by Monday. Mr. Ahmadi had assigned a historiographical paper, not on the French Revolution itself but on how accounts of it had shifted since 1800, and Jordan had spent two evenings staring at a blank document titled, simply, "draft." Now he stood in the Hall of Republics, where a glass case held a miniature guillotine no bigger than a bread knife and a bronze bust of a man with sideburns and a self-satisfied mouth.

Juliet found him there first. She was doing her paper on the Cold War and had finished early, which she mentioned twice. "Who's the guy?" she said, nodding at the bust.

"Someone French," Jordan said. The plaque read Adolphe Thiers, 1797 to 1877, statesman and historian. He wrote the label in his notebook because it seemed like the kind of detail that might count for something.

Noelle arrived holding three postcards she had no intention of buying. She read the plaque over Jordan's shoulder and said, "He ran France later, right? After he wrote about the Revolution. There's a whole thing about him online." She pulled out her phone, and the three of them leaned into the weak light of the case while she searched.

The museum's wifi was slow, but a digitized preface eventually loaded, and Noelle read part of it aloud in a flat, careful voice, the way she read proofs in geometry. Thiers's History of the French Revolution had been published from 1823 to 1827, the page said. In it he praised moderate leaders such as Mirabeau and Lafayette and condemned radicals such as Robespierre. "So he liked the ones who eased off," Juliet said, "and hated the one who didn't."

Jordan copied the sentence down. Then he sat on the bench opposite the case and looked at the guillotine again. He had been planning to write that historians simply disagreed about the Revolution, one side against the other, but that framing now seemed thin. Thiers had not just disagreed; he had judged, and the pattern of his judging had a shape. A man who would later govern France himself had spent his twenties lionizing the moderates, the men who tried to steer the thing, and had written of Robespierre as if virtue itself were a crime when combined with power. Jordan could not prove why Thiers judged that way, and he suspected the paper would be better if he admitted that.

"I need the gift shop's book section," he said. "They had a shelf of the cheap editions by the cafe."

The gift shop had one copy of a paperback anthology, and Jordan read the introduction standing between a rack of Eiffel Tower keychains and a cooler of overpriced water. The historian writing the introduction argued that later accounts, the Marxist ones and the revisionist ones that followed, kept circling back to the same fault line Thiers had drawn, even when they crossed it in different places. Jordan liked that image, though he worried it was too grandiose for a high school paper, a fault line running under two hundred years of argument. He wrote "fault line?" in the margin and underlined the question mark.

The loudspeaker announced that the museum would close in fifteen minutes. Juliet was already at the door. Noelle waited by the postcard rack, holding one of a building she could not identify. "You have an actual thesis now," she said. "That's more than you had this morning."

"I have half of one," Jordan said. "The other half is whether Thiers was describing the Revolution or describing what he wanted France to be, and I can't get there by Monday."

"Then write that you can't get there," she said. "Mr. Ahmadi keeps saying the honest papers are the interesting ones."

Jordan paid for the anthology at the register, and the cashier slid it into a bag with the museum's logo on it. Outside, the streetlights had come on, and Juliet was pretending to read the dedication on a plaque by the steps. Jordan took out his notebook on the museum's front stoop and, under the sentence about Thiers, wrote the first line of the draft: "The argument about the French Revolution began before the dust settled, and it has never once been only about the French Revolution."

He read it back to himself, decided it was probably too much, and crossed out "never once."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution in his 1863 book on drama technique.
story:
Liam had cleared the coffee table three times and it still wasn't a stage. The living room smelled faintly of the popcorn his dad had made and abandoned, and the sofa cushions he'd dragged to the floor kept sliding whenever anyone sat on them. His ten-minute play was due Friday, and it was currently eleven minutes of a boy standing at a window deciding whether to tell his mother he'd failed the audition. Even Liam found it boring, and he had lived it.

"Freytag," Nikhil said, flattening a napkin on the table and borrowing Caleigh's eyeliner to draw on it. "Drama camp, last summer. The pyramid." He sketched a lopsided triangle and sliced it into floors. "Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution, in his book on drama technique from 1863. Our instructor drew this exact thing on a napkin and I stole it. Well, I stole the idea of it." He tapped the middle. "Your play has no climax. It's all exposition. It's a very well-lit window."

Liam took the napkin and held it up to the lamp, as if light might reveal where the climax of his own life had been hiding. The problem was that the night in question had not felt like a pyramid. It had felt like standing in a hallway for a long time, and then a conversation that debilitated him more by being gentle than by being angry. "The climax can't be the audition," he said. "I don't even remember the audition. I remember the vending machine after. I bought a granola bar I didn't want."

"That's rising action," Caleigh said, mouth full of popcorn she had found somewhere. "Pathetic granola bar, that's rising action, that's good, that's real." She stood up on the coffee table, which groaned under her. "Where does your mom enter?"

They worked through it with the pyramid between them, sliding scenes up and down its floors like furniture. The vending machine went near the bottom. His mother's phone call, which in life had come two days later, got moved to the same night, because ten minutes forgives a person their chronology but not their shapelessness. By the time the lamp had gone amber with evening, the play had a climb to it. Liam could feel the stairs under the sentences.

Caleigh had been in the hallway getting water when she heard Liam say the mother's line, quietly, to nobody, trying it on. She stopped with the glass in her hand. He did the voice badly, an octave too high, and still something in it landed. He'd been so worried the play was too small, some parochial little kitchen drama about one boy and one bad Tuesday, that he hadn't noticed he'd made it kind. She came back in and said so, and he pulled a face like she'd called him a misanthrope, which made Nikhil laugh so hard he knocked the eyeliner off the table.

"Fine, it's kind," Liam said. "Kind and it has a structure. It can be both."

"Everything's both," Nikhil said. "That's the whole pyramid. Freytag knew."

The second half of the week they staged it. Nikhil played the mother with a dish towel on his head, which was either brilliant or a war crime, and Caleigh directed from the armchair with a spatula for a pointer. The sofa cushions became the hallway. The window became the window, since there was one. On Friday the actual audience arrived, eleven people squeezed into the living room, parents on folding chairs, and the play ran nine minutes and forty seconds because Liam had cut the granola bar after all. He stood in the hallway of his own making and told his mother he'd failed, and the room went quiet at the place the napkin said it would, and he felt the shape of it under him like a floor.

Afterward, people said nice things and ate the leftover popcorn, and Liam stood by the window with the napkin folded in his pocket. He still didn't know whether the real night had had a climax, or whether living things were too continuous for pyramids, or whether that even mattered now. Caleigh appeared beside him with the spatula still in her hand. "So," she said. "Next one's mine. And I want a volcano."

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Mishnah lists 39 categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath, which the rabbis linked to the kinds of work used to build the Tabernacle.
story:
Connor's uncle kept his books in the dining room, behind the glass doors of a cabinet that nobody was supposed to open with greasy fingers, and on the Friday that Connor's whole family came for dinner, he stood in front of it with his phone in his hand and his debate topic folded into his back pocket. The topic was whether an ancient religious rule still applied in modern life, and Mr. Li, who taught the class, had insisted that the argument had to come out of the text itself, not out of opinion. Connor had picked the Sabbath, mostly because it seemed easy, and had spent two days discovering it wasn't. His cousin had left a volume of the Mishnah on the table for him that afternoon, and now he had the book in one hand and his phone in the other, and the question he had typed into the search bar was whether switching on a phone counted as work.

"You're going to sit there reading during dinner," his mother said from the kitchen doorway, but she said it in the voice that meant she was willing to be argued with, so he had until the soup.

Anouk and Nikita arrived at six, because Connor had texted them that he was drowning. Anouk's family was secular and she said so at every opportunity, and Nikita's family was not, though he never said which way. The three of them had survived four years of debate tournaments together, and Anouk still believed every argument could be won by finding the definitions first. She dropped her bag on the couch, saw the Mishnah open on the table, and pulled it toward her.

"There's a list," Connor said, watching her find the page he'd marked with a receipt. "Thirty-nine categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath. The rabbis linked them to the kinds of work used to build the Tabernacle." He said it carefully, because he'd only read it an hour ago and wanted to make sure he had it exactly.

Anouk ran her finger down the page. "So none of it is just arbitrary. It's all pegged to one thing." She looked up. "That's actually a way better argument than the one you had."

"It is or it isn't," Nikita said. He'd gone quiet by the window, which Nikita sometimes did, and Connor had learned not to read it as anything. "People argue about the list all the time. That's kind of the point of it."

From the doorway, Connor watched his uncle come in from the kitchen carrying soup bowls, and it occurred to him, with a small lurch, that his uncle had never once told him what to think about any of this. The book had been left on the table. That was all.

Anouk had known Connor since ninth grade, when he'd been all showmanship and no substance, and she'd watched him get more cerebral each year until sometimes she wanted to shake him and tell him a feeling was allowed to be a reason. Now she watched him hold the phone over the open Mishnah like he was weighing them against each other, literally, one in each hand, and she thought he was about to make the mistake of picking a side too early.

"Say the phone thing out loud," she said. "Both sides. I'll tell you which one you believe."

"Okay. Against applying it: the categories are about building a tent, spinning wool, lighting fires. Nobody in the Mishnah could have imagined a circuit. For applying it: an electric current completes something, the rabbis thought about completion as work, so a completed circuit is work." He set the phone down. "The second one is more interesting. But I don't know if interesting means right."

"That's the first honest thing you've said all week," Nikita said, and for once he was smiling.

They ate dinner late, and Connor's uncle asked, between the soup and the main course, how the debate was going, and Connor said the thing he'd decided was true: that the rule was built to be argued with, that the argument was the observance, maybe, and then he stopped, because he heard how much he was prognosticating and how little he actually knew. His uncle nodded slowly and said, "You could say that at the dinner table too," and passed him the bread.

That night, after Anouk and Nikita had gone home and the dishes were done, Connor sat at the dining room table with the volume open again. He'd written PROBITY at the top of his notes, then crossed it out, then written it again, because the word kept insisting on itself: honesty about what he could prove. He could prove the list, the thirty-nine, the Tabernacle. He could not prove what the rabbis would say about his phone, glowing there beside the book.

He left the phone face down and read one more page by lamplight.

"You're going to fall asleep at the table," his mother said from the stairs.

"One more page," he said.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can.
story:
Vanessa had spread the two articles across the kitchen table like cards she did not want to play. One, from a psychology journal, claimed that lessons taught outdoors improved children's attention afterward; the other, from an education journal, found no such improvement in a yearlong study of two schools. The assignment from Mr. Almeida asked for a critical review comparing the two, and she had promised herself she would start it Saturday morning, before her mother woke and turned the kitchen into a place for other purposes. It was now Saturday morning, and her mother was frying eggs six feet away, and the articles still said opposite things.

The problem was not that they disagreed. The problem was that both looked convincing. The outdoor-learning study had tested only forty children in a montane forest program, spruce and thin cold air, which sounded vivid and small at once. The yearlong study had followed hundreds of children but in ordinary schoolyards, and Vanessa kept circling the word "ordinary" as though it were hiding something. She wrote "sample size?" on a napkin and then crossed it out, because she did not actually know whether size settled anything. She had a memory of choosing the easier essay topic in grade ten and regretting it all semester, and she did not want to choose wrong again, but choosing right here seemed to require a kind of discernment she had not been taught.

Her phone buzzed. Andrew, from her class: "Almeida says we can bring drafts Monday. Have you even picked a side?"

She typed "no" and then deleted it, because it wasn't true that she needed a side. She needed a way to stand between them. She typed instead: "coming over?"

He arrived with his own articles shoved in a backpack, the same two, and he dropped into the chair across from her and stole a piece of toast off her plate with the ease of someone who had done it for years. "I'm going with the outdoor one," he said. "It's shorter."

"That's your criterion?"

"It's a criterion." He tapped her first article. "Forty kids, though. That's like nothing."

"So the big study wins?"

"The big study is boring."

Her mother set a plate of eggs in front of him without being asked, cajoling him to eat properly the way she cajoled everyone, as though good food were a position she could argue him into. Vanessa stared past both of them at the laptop screen. Forty kids versus hundreds of kids, one result versus its opposite, and neither article explained how she was supposed to weigh them. It felt like being handed two witnesses who swore differently and no judge.

Then she thought, slowly, that other people must have noticed the disagreement before her. Other studies must exist. Other researchers must have looked at the same question, over and over, in forests and schoolyards and wherever else. She opened a search window and typed the question itself, not the article titles, and added a word she had seen once in a footnote and not understood: "pooled."

The result that came up first was called a meta-analysis. She said the word out loud, flat, testing it. "A meta-analysis," Andrew repeated around his toast. "What is that, like an analysis of an analysis?"

"Sort of," she said, reading. "It combines the results of many studies on the same question." The screen said more, and she read it twice because it mattered: all those studies together, pooled, estimated the overall effect more precisely than any single study could. Not a new experiment. A way of holding every experiment at once and seeing what they added up to. She sat back. "So one study with forty kids isn't the whole answer. Even the big one isn't. Somebody already put them all together."

"Convenient," Andrew said. "Somebody did your homework."

"Somebody did the homework of the entire field." She was already skimming the meta-analysis, twenty-some studies listed in a table, her two articles both there, side by side, names she recognized like people spotted in a crowd. The pooled estimate sat somewhere between certainty and nothing: a small improvement, held loosely. Small, but not zero. Not zero, but small.

"So which one was right?" Andrew leaned over her shoulder.

"Neither. Both. The forest study overshot because it was tiny, and the yearlong study couldn't see it because its schoolyards were, I don't know, muted." She frowned at her own sentence. "I don't love that word. But that's the shape of it. The answer is smaller than the first article says and more real than the second one admits."

Her mother, wiping the counter, said, "In my day we just wrote what the teacher wanted."

Vanessa didn't answer, because she was writing now, fast, the pen hurting her fingers. The review was taking a shape she hadn't planned: not a verdict on the two articles but a chain of reasoning about why they diverged and what a reader should hold onto. She gave the small effect its due and then gave her uncertainty its due too, because the pooled estimate was an average over wildly different places, and she could not tell from her kitchen table whether a montane forest program and a concrete schoolyard belonged in the same average at all. Maybe they did. Maybe that was the whole point of pooling. She left the question in the draft, marked with an asterisk, and did not resolve it.

Andrew read over her shoulder, still chewing. "You're allowed to end with a question?"

"It's not a question. It's a stated uncertainty. There's a difference."

"Is there?"

She pulled the laptop back toward herself and typed the asterisk note into a real sentence. "I'll find out Monday."

He laughed and took another piece of her toast, and she let him, watching the cursor blink at the end of the line she wasn't sure about yet.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year.
story:
Isabella found Mr. Flores by the punch bowl, which was actually a cooler with lemonade in it, and which he was guarding with the mild belligerence of a man who had broken up too many parties in his career as a chemistry teacher. The party was in Tanisha's backyard, strung with lights that her father had hung badly, sagging between the fence and the garage like sentences he had started and abandoned. Somebody's cousin had made a playlist that kept skipping. Everyone was eighteen hours past graduation and still wearing pieces of it, sashes draped over lawn chairs, one corsage wilting in a cup.

"You should be dancing," Mr. Flores said.

"I should be doing a lot of things." Isabella held out her cup and he poured, unimpressed. Around the yard, people she had known since seventh grade were shouting at each other over the music, and she was counting them without meaning to. Dawson was by the fence with his guitar, playing to an audience of two freshmen who had snuck in. Tanisha was orchestrating a group photo, herding people by the shoulders. The class had been four hundred and eleven at ninth-grade orientation. She remembered the number because they had stood in the gym in rows and the principal had said it like a promise.

Later, when the cake came out, Tanisha climbed onto a lawn chair to make a toast and got halfway through it before she stopped. "Where's Marisol?" she said, not into the microphone of her cupped hands but to Isabella, quietly, stepping down. "And the Okafor twins. And that kid Denny who used to eat lunch outside the band room."

"They didn't graduate," Isabella said. She had learned it that morning, accidentally, scrolling on her phone while her mother made breakfast. The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year. She had read it twice and then done the arithmetic on the back of a cereal box, because four hundred and eleven times thirteen percent was a number of people, was roughly fifty-three people, was a busload, was Denny eating alone outside the band room while she walked past with her friends every day for four years.

"So they're just gone," Tanisha said. "Nobody said anything."

"We litigated it," Dawson said, arriving with his guitar still strapped on. "Every quarter. Attendance appeals, credit recovery, the whole thing. Mr. Flores, tell her."

Mr. Flores looked at the lemonade. "The system caught some of them," he said. "The ones it missed, we all missed." He wouldn't say more than that, and Isabella didn't ask him to, because she suspected that whatever he knew, he had already turned it over for years, and it hadn't gotten lighter.

She walked to the fence where the lights sagged lowest and took out her phone. There was a message she had drafted to Denny months ago, in February, after she'd seen him carrying his skateboard through the snow past the library. She had never sent it. It said: "I don't know if you remember me, we had bio together freshman year, you told me the mitochondria diagram looked like a Rorschach test and Mr. Flores laughed even though he pretended not to. I noticed you're not around anymore. I should have noticed earlier. If you want a coffee or whatever, no speech, I'm around." She had been proud of the line about the Rorschach test. She had also been afraid it was a speech, that the whole message was a small performance of caring, and so she had kept it in drafts like a coin she was too superstititious to spend.

She sent it now. The yard behind her was loud, the cake was being cut, Tanisha was calling her name for the photo. The message sat on the screen with the word Sending underneath it, then nothing, the way the phone just goes quiet when it's done, giving no opinion about what happens next.

In the group photo, Isabella stood at the end of the row, squinting into the flash, and she thought about how the picture would show four hundred minus fifty-three faces, all smiling, and it would look like a complete thing. It wasn't a lie exactly. She had worked hard; they all had; the caps had gone up into the air for real. But underneath the picture there was this other accounting, the missing faces as a kind of substrate the visible ones rested on, and she could not decide whether remembering that made the night heavier or more honest. She held still while Tanisha counted down from three.

Her phone buzzed against her hip. She did not look at it until after the flash, and then only long enough to see the name, and the two words, and the question mark at the end of them. She typed back, "The one on Mercer, tomorrow at four," and pressed send before she could litigate it with herself again, and walked back toward the cake with the phone warm in her hand.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Upstage means away from the audience and downstage means toward it; the terms come from old raked stages that sloped down toward the audience.
story:
Kaitlyn had been given the one-act because she was the only one who volunteered, which was not the same as being chosen, and she felt the difference every afternoon in the school auditorium like a draft from the proscenium arch. The play was eleven pages long. Her cast was Kobe, who had auditioned as a joke and then discovered he liked being watched, and Pyper, who had memorized everyone's lines including the stage directions. Kaitlyn stood in the third row with a clipboard and asked them to move, and they did not move.

"The scene is a fight," she said. "You can't have a fight standing in the same spot for four minutes."

"It's a verbal fight," Kobe said. "Verbal fights happen standing still. Watch any documentary."

Pyper, who had opinions about character motivation she shared without being asked, said the stillness was a choice, that her character was frozen by grief. Kaitlyn said her character was a landlord. She wanted them crossed downstage by the second beat, Kobe near the edge of the stage, Pyper upstage near the window flat, so that when the truth about the eviction came out Pyper would have to travel toward him and the distance would mean something. She had drawn it in pencil. She had redrawn it twice. They looked at the pencil marks the way people look at weather.

Ms. Wilson, who supervised the auditorium on Tuesdays and Thursdays while grading papers in the back row, had told her on the first day that directing was mostly logistics, that the disbursement of time and attention was the real job, and that the art happened in the gaps if it happened at all. Kaitlyn had found this either cynical or the truest thing anyone had said to her all year, and she had not decided which. What she knew was that she had two weeks, one working light cue, and a lead actor who would not walk six feet toward the audience.

The breakthrough, such as it was, came sideways. Her mother's friend from the community theatre had offered the cast a backstage tour, and on Saturday they stood in the wings while a man in paint-stained overalls rearranged flats. Kobe asked him why everyone kept calling the back of the stage up when the floor was flat as a table, and before the man could answer, Kaitlyn heard herself say it: upstage means away from the audience and downstage means toward it, and the terms come from old raked stages that sloped down toward the audience. She had read it at one in the morning in a forum thread about Shakespeare, and it had stuck the way tangential facts stick to her, uselessly and forever. The man in overalls nodded and went back to his flats.

From Kobe's side of it, the whole thing had seemed like a hobby Kaitlyn was suffering through on everyone's behalf, pencils and clipboards and a theory about where people should stand. He had assumed the directions were arbitrary, one more rule invented by adults to make teenagers feel wrong-footed. But standing in that community theatre he looked down at the sloped floor, imagined the audience below him and the back wall above, and understood for the first time that the words had a shape to them, that the stage was a hill whether or not the school's floor admitted it. He thought about Kaitlyn wanting him lower, closer to the audience, exposed. He had assumed she wanted to embarrass him. It had not seriously occurred to him that she might want him seen, which was different, and he spent the bus ride home turning that over without resolving it.

On Monday he came into the auditorium early, before Pyper, and walked the marks Kaitlyn had drawn. He was careful about it at first, the way he was careful about anything that looked like effort, and then less careful. When Kaitlyn arrived he was standing downstage right, near the edge, and he said, "Okay. The landlord scene. I'll take the downhill." She looked at him for a second too long, then wrote something on her clipboard, which he understood to be her way of not making it a moment.

The rehearsal that followed was the first one that ran like a rehearsal instead of a negotiation. Pyper found that her grief, or the landlord's, played differently with room to move through, and Kaitlyn discovered that if she stopped explaining why a movement mattered and just said when, the actors stopped arguing with the reason. There was still the problem of the third scene, where neither of them had a better idea than the one in the pencil, and Kaitlyn wrote it on a sticky note for tomorrow. Ms. Wilson, grading in the back row, did not look up, but she had stopped grading somewhere in the second beat, and her pen was resting on the same word it had been resting on ten minutes before.

What stayed uncertain, for Kaitlyn, was whether any of it would survive an audience. Two weeks was nothing; the tour of that other stage had told her how little she knew, how much of directing she was inventing from fragments. But when Pyper crossed toward Kobe on the eviction line, and Kobe, planted near the audience on the imagined slope, did not move away from her, Kaitlyn stood up in the third row and said, "Again. From the top. And this time, Kobe, don't blink."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
Elijah showed up to the community center gym ten minutes early, the way he had every Tuesday since November, and taped the roster sheet to the corkboard by the water fountain. Twelve names for the winter league, twelve boys who had mostly never played together before. Denver arrived second, as usual, and read the sheet over his shoulder.

"You put yourself at point again," Denver said.

"I'm the one who volunteers to run drills. Nobody else wants it."

Denver rolled his ball toward the far hoop and didn't answer, which Elijah took as an answer anyway.

For the first month the team was easy. Nobody knew anybody well enough to argue. They lost three games by close margins and Emie, who had played two seasons at his old school, kept quiet in the huddles and shot only when nobody passed to him, which was often. By January they had won two, and something about winning loosened everyone's tongues. Denver started calling his own plays. Emie started refusing them, loudly. In the third week of January, during a timeout against St. Brigid's, Denver said Emie passed like he was afraid of the ball, and Emie said Denver's plays were all about Denver, and Mr. Santoso, who refereed the community league on Thursdays, had to step onto the floor and separate them before it got physical.

Elijah's mother had a rule about walking off anger, so he walked home the long way, past the shuttered pharmacy, and when he got in he found a message printed out and left on his desk. His mother did that, printed texts and emails and left them where he'd find them. This one was from Denver, sent an hour earlier.

"I'm not quitting," it read, "but I'm not running drills for people who don't listen. You can have Wednesday. Also I'm sorry about the St. Brigid's thing. Not the argument, the timing. Do what you want with that."

Elijah read it twice, then sat with his shoes still on. He had a psychology textbook from the library on his desk, borrowed for a class project on persuasion, and while avoiding that project he had wandered into the chapter on groups. He turned back to the page he'd flagged without knowing why. Bruce Tuckman had proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing. The word "storming" had struck him as almost comically literal, given the week he'd had. He read the four stages again, then copied them onto the back of a receipt, then felt vaguely foolish about copying something he could photograph, and photographed it anyway.

At Wednesday's practice he taped a new sheet to the corkboard. Under the roster he had written the four stages, the name Tuckman, the year, and nothing else. Emie arrived first, read it, and squinted.

"What is this, a history lesson?"

"It's where we are," Elijah said. "Stage two. Apparently stage two is normal."

Denver came in with his ball under his arm and stood in front of the sheet long enough that Elijah thought he might tear it down. Instead he said, "So what's stage three," and Elijah said "norming," and Denver said "which means what, exactly," and Elijah admitted he didn't fully know, because the textbook gave examples from offices and therapy groups and he wasn't sure how much carried over to a rec league in a church basement with a leaky radiator. That admission seemed to matter more than the list did. They ran drills, all three of them calling changes out loud, badly at first.

They lost their next game by two, won the one after by nine, and finished the season in the middle of the standings, which nobody celebrated. On the last Tuesday, Emie asked Elijah whether he thought they had actually reached stage four or whether they'd spent the whole season stuck between stages and just gotten used to each other. Elijah said he genuinely didn't know, that the model was probably too clean for a thing as messy as twelve boys and a borrowed gym, and Emie nodded as though this were the answer he'd wanted.

Mr. Santoso found Elijah after the final game, folding the nets, and held out a registration form for the spring league. Twelve slots, one team, Elijah's name written at the top as coach. "You volunteer for everything," Mr. Santoso said. "So volunteer."

Elijah looked at the form. Stage one. Forming. A whole new team that would like him, and argue with him, and settle around him, and he would be the one standing at the corkboard trying to keep twelve boys from tearing each other apart, week after week, for the length of another winter.

He took the pen.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In a presidential system, the president is elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term and cannot be removed simply because the legislature disagrees with them.
story:
The folding chairs in the city hall lobby had been arranged in a horseshoe, and by seven o'clock most of them were full. Nathan sat at the edge of the horseshoe with a printout on his knees, a study sheet for the model parliament tryouts on Saturday, and he was on his fourth read of the same paragraph when Audrey-Anne dropped into the chair beside him with two hot chocolates and handed him one.

"You look like a man being slowly crushed by paper," she said.

"It's the comparative section." He turned the sheet so she could see it. "They give you a scenario and you have to argue both sides. Parliamentary versus presidential." He took the cup. Steam fogged the top line of the page, and he wiped it with his sleeve. "I know the parliamentary half. My uncle in Manchester used to complain about it every Christmas, no-confidence votes and all that. The other half I only know from the news, and the news isn't a system, it's weather."

Across the horseshoe, Milla was waving. She had claimed a spot near the radiator and was saving it for the three of them; the meeting about the youth budget hadn't started, and Mr. Islam, who ran the youth council, was still unfolding his notes at the front table. Nathan and Audrey-Anne crossed the room, stepping over bags and an abandoned stroller, and settled in as Milla divided a bag of pretzels into three uneven piles without being asked.

"I heard you from the door," Milla said. "Presidential what?"

"Systems. How they pick the head of government." Nathan looked at his sheet again, embarrassed by how thin his margin notes were. "In the parliamentary thing, like Britain, the party that wins the legislature gets to form the government, so the prime minister comes out of parliament. And if parliament turns on the prime minister, out the prime minister goes. Fine. I can say that."

"That's how it works back home for my aunt too," Audrey-Anne said. "She's always on the phone about whatever the government lost this week. But say the other one."

Nathan looked up at the ceiling, where a vestigial smoke detector hung dead in its bracket beside a newer one, and admitted it. "I can't, really. Not the whole shape of it. I know there's an election, but I can't figure out whether the legislature can throw the president out when they get sick of him, and that seems like the entire point."

Milla tilted her head. "My dad used to lecture about this at dinner. He'd say the president is elected separately from the legislature. Separate ballot, separate contest. And then he'd do the thing with the saltshaker." She set the saltshaker from the pretzel bag in the middle of the radiator ledge. "President. Fixed term. He'd say you can't just reach over and take it off the table because congress is annoyed with it. It sits there until the term runs out."

Nathan wrote it down, then looked at what he'd written. "So the legislature can disagree all it wants, and the president still serves the whole term?"

"Unless the term ends," Milla said. "That's it. That's the saltshaker."

"So disagreement isn't enough," Nathan said slowly, mostly to himself. "That's why the two arguments can't line up. In one system the leader stands on the legislature's floor and falls when the floor shifts. In the other the leader has a separate mandate and a clock, and the clock is the only thing that runs out on schedule." He underlined the sentence twice, and Audrey-Anne leaned over to read it.

"That's better than the platitude in your textbook," she said. "Paragraph four. It says something like 'different democracies reflect different values,' which tells me nothing while sounding wise." She tapped the page. "Yours tells me what actually happens."

Mr. Islam called the meeting to order, and for an hour they went through the youth budget line by line, the noise of it warm and slightly argumentative, someone's chair squeaking whenever the pool hours came up. Nathan voted on the pool hours. He passed Milla the pen she'd dropped. When the meeting wound down and people began stacking chairs, he stayed in his seat, spread the study sheet across two chairs, and read his own note again, testing it.

"Here's what I still can't settle," he said when the two of them came back for him. "Which one I'd argue for. If the leader can be pulled down by the legislature, then the government answers to the chamber and the chamber answers to voters, which feels responsive. But it can atrophy into a revolving door, governments collapsing every winter, and nobody's responsible for anything long. If the president sits out a fixed term no matter what the legislature thinks, then at least somebody is answerable for four years, and you know exactly who to blame. Except if things go truly wrong, you wait. You just wait." He folded the sheet, unfolded it, folded it again. "I keep deciding, and then deciding the other way."

"Then argue that," Audrey-Anne said, hauling her bag onto her shoulder. "Saturday. Say you can see both and then tell them which one wins by a nose. Judges love a person who's actually thought."

Milla picked up the saltshaker and pressed it into Nathan's hand. "Take it. For the desk."

He held it up to the lobby's fluorescent light, salt shifting inside like a small grey hourglass, and dropped it into his pocket with the folded sheet.

"Fixed term," he said, and followed them out through the glass doors into the cold.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: An arbitration clause requires the parties to settle disputes through private arbitration instead of in court, and in the US it is often paired with a waiver of class-action lawsuits.
story:
Stella read the phrase "binding arbitration" three times on the driving school's clipboard before she understood that she was not just signing up for lessons. She was signing away something.

The office smelled of burnt coffee and vinyl, and behind the counter a fan turned its head slowly from side to side like a teacher deciding whom to blame. Her mother had dropped her at the curb with a check and the words "just sign whatever, sweetheart," which was exactly the kind of instruction Stella distrusted on principle. The form was four pages. The first two were ordinary: name, address, emergency contact, consent for a minor to operate a vehicle with an instructor. Frederique had signed hers in under a minute last week and had already posted a video of herself parallel parking between two traffic cones, captioned "law of the jungle." Stella read on.

Page three said that any dispute arising from the contract would be settled through private arbitration instead of in court, and that the signer waived participation in any class-action lawsuit. She looked up. "What does arbitration mean?" she asked the woman at the desk, who shrugged without lifting her eyes from her phone. Behind Stella, a boy was arguing about whether his coupon had expired. It was Frederique who answered, appearing beside her with a bottle of orange juice and the timing of someone who had been waiting for Stella to reach page three.

"It means you can't sue them," Frederique said. "You agreed. Check your little paragraph." Frederique had found out the hard way, which was to say the funny way: last summer, scrolling through the terms of a photo app at her kitchen table, she had clicked "I agree" to forty pages she had never read, and when the app glitched and ate three months of her portfolio, her cousin, who was in law school, had laughed and told her she'd signed away her day in court. The whole family now ascribed Frederique's bad luck to that app, the way other families ascribed weather to saints.

"I didn't agree yet," Stella said. "That's the difference between us."

"That's the difference between us and everyone," Frederique said, and stole a sip of Stella's water.

Ms. Barrett, the owner, came out of the back room with a stack of traffic cones under one arm. Stella had met her once at the open house, where Ms. Barrett had let a nervous Asha practice steering in the parking lot for twenty extra minutes after everyone else left, walking beside the car with her hand hovering near the hood like a parent teaching a child to ride a bike. She was not, Stella thought, an obvious villain. She stopped when she saw Stella holding the form away from her body, at reading distance, like a fish she was unsure about.

"Most parents just sign it," Ms. Barrett said, not unkindly. "The insurance company requires it. It's standard."

"Standard isn't the same as fair," Stella said, and heard her own voice wobble between bravado and honest question.

Ms. Barrett set down the cones. "You're right that it's not the same," she said. "But I'd point out you get something too. Six lessons, a certified instructor, a car with dual brakes. You're exchanging a right you'll probably never need for a service you definitely do." She said it lightly, the way you'd discuss the weather, and Stella felt the pull of it, the tidy logic of exchange. Contracts were just promises with teeth. Everybody made them. She wanted to drive. She wanted it with a somatic insistence she could feel in her hands, which had been gripping an imaginary wheel since she was eleven, when her grandfather let her steer his truck down the empty dirt lane behind the orchard and she had screamed with exhilaration the whole way while he laughed and worked the pedals.

"Can I cross out that part?" Stella asked.

"You can ask." Ms. Barrett took the form and read the paragraph herself, slowly, as if meeting it for the first time, and Stella watched her face do something complicated. "If you were eighteen, you could negotiate. At sixteen, your mother's signature is what binds you. She'd have to come in." She handed the clipboard back. "Or you can sign, and I'll note that you read it, which frankly nobody does, and which I'll admit I like seeing."

Frederique leaned against the counter. "Sign it. You've wanted this since the truck."

Stella stood there with the pen. She thought about her mother at the curb, about the app Frederique could not sue, about Ms. Barrett's hand hovering near Asha's hood. Two things seemed true at once: that giving up a right casually was how people ended up with none, and that a person could refuse every agreement and never get anywhere at all. She could not make those two truths hold hands, and she suspected they never would.

She signed her name, then, in the margin beside the arbitration clause, in small careful letters, wrote "read and objected, 16, minor." Ms. Barrett looked at it for a long moment and stamped the form without a word. Then she handed Stella the keys to the practice car.

"Cones are already set up," she said. "Try not to hit the second one. It's my favorite."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 2022 the United Kingdom had three prime ministers, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak, without a general election, because the governing party changed its leader.
story:
The line outside the council chamber at city hall moved slowly, and Victor shifted his folder from one arm to the other, checking for the third time that his notes were in order. He was there for the youth civic forum, a Saturday program Ms. Berg had badgered half the senior class into attending, and his assignment was to present a comparison of how a parliamentary system and a presidential system each choose and remove a head of government. He understood the mechanics well enough on paper. What he did not yet have was the part that would make anyone care.

Camilla found him near the sign-in table, unwinding a scarf stamped with small raindrops. "You look like you're about to defend a thesis," she said.

"I might be." He tapped the folder. "Presidents are elected separately from the legislature, fixed terms, removal by impeachment. Prime ministers come out of the parliament, and the parliament can pull them down whenever it loses confidence." He said it all in one breath, the way he'd rehearsed it on the bus, and heard how flat it sounded even as he said it.

"That's the whole thing?"

"That's the whole thing on paper. It's the difference between a locked door and a revolving one, and I can't figure out which is a virtue."

Camilla pulled him toward the seats along the wall. "My aunt lives in Leeds," she said. "You know what happened over there? In 2022 the United Kingdom had three prime ministers, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak, all in one year, and none of it went to a general election. The governing party just changed its leader." She said it lightly, the way she reported most things, but Victor sat forward. Sharon, arriving behind them with two coffees, overheard the last sentence and frowned. "Three in a year? Without anyone voting?"

"That's what my aunt said. She kept a newspaper clipping."

Victor turned the fact over in his head while Ms. Berg called the forum to order. He had written his comparison as if one system were obviously tidier than the other, and here was a case that unsettled the tidiness. In a presidential system a country could be saddled with a leader it despised for years, waiting out a fixed term, unless the arduous machinery of impeachment could be cranked into motion, which it rarely could. In a parliamentary system the door swung the other way, so freely that a party alone could swap heads of government midstream. The revolving door emancipated a country from a failed leader between elections, but the same freedom meant the voters' original choice could be quietly overridden by insiders. Both facts were true at once, and his outline had only room for one.

When the floor opened for the student presentations, Victor went up with his folder and then, unexpectedly, set it half aside. "I prepared a comparison," he said, "and I'm going to give it, but I want to start with something a classmate told me ten minutes ago." He recounted what Camilla had said, watching Sharon nod in the second row to confirm she'd heard it too. "Three prime ministers in the UK in 2022, Johnson, Truss, then Sunak, no general election, because the governing party changed its leader. If that had happened under presidential rules, it would have been a constitutional crisis. Under parliamentary rules, it was a Tuesday."

A man in the audience, someone's father maybe, called out that it sounded like the parties were treating the country as their private property. Victor was ready with the term for that, one Ms. Berg had made them memorize and one he'd privately found ugly and useful. "A party that treats the leadership as its own possession is basically an egoist with a membership list," he said, and a ripple of laughter went through the chamber. "But the same rules let a country correct a mistake without waiting years for a fixed term to expire. So which fault matters more, the arrogance of insiders or the paralysis of locks?"

Ms. Berg did not rescue him. She sat at the side table with her pen still, which Victor had learned was her way of saying continue. He laid out the two columns plainly: the presidential system elects its head separately, with a fixed term, and removal requires impeachment; the parliamentary system's head emerges from the elected chamber and can fall to a vote of no confidence. Then he said the part he had only worked out in the previous fifteen minutes. "I came here today convinced one of these was better. I don't think I can say that anymore. The parliamentary system is faster and more accountable to the moment; the presidential system is slower and more accountable to the calendar. I trust the moment more when I'm angry and the calendar more when I'm calm, which tells me the answer has something to do with what a country is feeling."

During the question period a girl two rows back asked which he'd choose if he had to. Victor looked at his folder, at the neat outline he'd written on the bus, and found he didn't want to flatten what he'd just built. "I'd want a system that can remove a failing leader quickly but can't remove him secretly," he said. "I don't know that one exists. Maybe the honest answer is that every constitution is a compromise between speed and stability, and the 2022 example shows how much speed a system can absorb before people start asking who actually voted for this."

Afterward, Camilla caught him by the doors, and Sharon trailed behind with the remaining coffee. "That was trenchant," Camilla said, "for a Saturday morning." Victor laughed and admitted the best part of it had been her aunt's newspaper clipping. "Tell her I owe her a citation." Outside, the steps of city hall were bright and cold, and Sharon held the door while he stuffed the folder, unused outline and all, deep into his bag.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In a standard repayment mortgage, early monthly payments go mostly toward interest, and later payments go mostly toward paying down the amount borrowed.
story:
The real estate office smelled of burnt coffee and carpet cleaner, and Laura sat in a plastic chair by the window while her mother signed papers at the front desk. They had come to settle the deposit on the new apartment, two months of rent held back in case they damaged anything, which her mother called insurance and the lease called security. Through the glass, Laura watched a woman argue with a man about a fridge that had come with the unit and now, apparently, would not.

The cousin, Anjali, was already there when they arrived, sitting across from an agent with a folder of her own. Anjali was twenty-five and had bought a small house in the spring, and she was the reason Laura had started paying attention to any of this. Laura had overheard her on the phone last month, saying something that made no sense: five years of payments, and she still owed almost everything she'd borrowed.

"Tell her," Anjali said now, waving Laura over. "You're good with numbers. Make him explain it to me like I'm not an idiot."

The agent, a phlegmatic man with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead, slid a sheet across the desk. It was a schedule, rows of months, and next to each month two columns: interest and principal. Laura leaned in. In the first rows almost all of the payment sat in the interest column. Far down the page, in the rows for year twenty-something, the columns flipped, and most of the money went to the principal, the actual amount borrowed.

"That's the part that killed me," Anjali said. "I've been paying every month, on time, five years of checks. And I look at my statement and the balance barely moved."

Laura ran her finger down the column. "So the early payments mostly just cover interest," she said slowly, testing it. "And the later ones mostly pay down what you owe." She looked up at the agent. "That's a standard repayment mortgage?"

"That's a standard repayment mortgage," he said, and turned back to his screen.

Anjali threw up her hands. "So I've been renting money, basically. Five years and I own, what, a doorknob and a porch step."

Laura didn't answer right away, because she was still looking at the sheet, wondering whether the order mattered, whether the bank got paid first or whether the interest itself was what made the early years so thin. She couldn't tell from the numbers alone, and the sheet didn't say. The fact of it sat there plainly, but the why underneath it stayed out of reach, like a machine whose throughput you could measure without ever seeing inside. She filed the question away for later, for the internet, for a night when she couldn't sleep.

Her mother called her over to the desk then. The new apartment wanted first month, last month, and the deposit together, and the total on the receipt was more than Laura had imagined a move could cost. Her mother counted out the cashier's check, wrote the numbers in her small neat hand, and said what she always said, that renting was throwing money into a hole. But Anjali's schedule was still on the other desk, and Laura thought about how her mother's landlord had probably used thirty years of rent checks to pay off a building, the early ones mostly interest, and now the rent was pure gain. Nothing was a hole, exactly. Everything was a pipe, and the question was who stood at which end of it.

"You could prognosticate the whole housing market from that one sheet," Anjali said behind her, half joking, gathering her folder. "Or you could just cry. I might do both."

Laura laughed and folded her copy of the lease into her backpack, careful with the crease, because something in her wanted to keep it flat. Later she would take out the amortization schedule Anjali had photocopied for her, five years and a doorknob, and lay it beside her mother's receipt on the kitchen table to see what matched and what didn't.

At the door, Anjali paused. "When you buy a place, call me first. We'll read everything before we sign."

"Deal," Laura said, and pushed the door open into the parking lot, where the August heat hit her face like a wall.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Percent yield is the actual mass of product obtained divided by the theoretical yield, multiplied by 100.
story:
The kitchen at his grandfather's house still smelled of coffee and pencil shavings, and Jordan spread his notebook across the oilcloth the way he had when he was ten, doing long division while his grandfather read the paper. On a saucer beside him sat the crystals, pale blue and clumped like frost, the whole project he had spent six weeks growing for the science fair. He had weighed them that morning at school: 4.2 grams. Mckenna, across the table, had her own notebook open and was not looking at it.

"You need the molar mass first," Jordan said. "That's the whole trick. You divide the mass of what you started with by the molar mass, and that gives you moles, and the moles tell you how much product you should have gotten."

"Say that like I'm a person who failed the quiz."

He wrote the numbers out slowly, the way Ms. Demir had shown them in the unit they'd all suffered through in March. Twenty grams of alum to start. Molar mass, 474 grams per mole. "So twenty divided by four seventy-four," he said, working it through. "That's about point zero four two moles. And one mole of alum gives one mole of the crystal product, so theoretically I should have ended up with point zero four two moles of crystals too." He multiplied by the molar mass of the product and circled the answer: 19.9 grams, give or take.

Mckenna leaned over the saucer and tapped the blue clumps with one fingernail. "So where's the other fifteen grams."

"That's what I can't figure out." His grandfather came in from the porch and settled into his chair without a word, saturnine as always behind his reading glasses, the kind of man who could disapprove of a whole generation with one slow exhale. Jordan waited for him to pontificate about how in his day students did their arithmetic without calculators, but he only turned a page.

Jordan had been turning the problem over since fourth period. Ms. Demir had looked at his crystals, then at his lab sheet, and had said only, "You know there's a way to put a number on the gap." No elaboration. She did that, dropped a door into the floor and walked away. Cassidy had offered to help him figure it out after school, and Jordan had said no, thanks, he had it. That had been a mistake, possibly. He and Cassidy had barely spoken since Cassidy partnered with someone else on the last lab, and Jordan had taken it personally, and now there was this cold weeks-long thing between them that neither of them had named.

He flipped back through his notes. Somewhere in the chapter review there had been a phrase. Actual mass, divided by something. He found it, read it twice, then set the calculator down and just looked at the crystals, the saucer, the scale reading he had written on his wrist at school and transferred, sweatily, to the page.

"Okay," he said. "I think I've got it. Percent yield. Percent yield is the actual mass of product you got divided by the theoretical yield, times a hundred." He wrote the formula out, then his numbers underneath: 4.2 on top, 19.9 on the bottom. "So that's twenty-one percent. Twenty-one percent, Mckenna. I grew a fifth of what I was supposed to grow."

"Is that bad?"

"It's information." He was surprised by how the number settled something in him. For six weeks the crystals had been a vague embarrassment, a jar of almost-nothing on his shelf, and now they were twenty-one percent, a quantity, something he could stand next to and argue with. He thought about texting Cassidy. Not an apology exactly, because he still wasn't sure he'd been wrong to want to do it alone, only wrong about how he'd said it. Maybe just the number. Twenty-one percent. Cassidy would know what it meant without being told, and would probably send back something sarcastic, and that would be the rapprochement, small and sidelong, the way things between them had always moved.

His grandfather lowered the paper an inch. "Twenty-one percent," he said. It wasn't a question. Jordan nodded. The old man studied the crystals for a long moment, then the page of arithmetic, and then he reached over and turned the notebook toward himself, and Jordan let him, and outside the screen door a lawnmower started up somewhere down the street, cutting through the quiet.

Mckenna pulled out her phone. "Take a picture of the saucer with the number. Send it to Cassidy." She said it casually, eyes on the crystals, as if the name had cost nothing.

Jordan typed the message: twenty-one percent. want to see what went wrong with me? He held his thumb over send while the coffee maker gurgled in the corner and the blue clumps sat catching the window light, and his grandfather watched him over the top of the paper, and then he pressed it.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When entering a highway, drivers use the acceleration lane to reach a speed close to that of highway traffic before merging, since merging slowly forces others to brake.
story:
The cones had been his grandfather's idea, six of them salvaged from a road crew's discard pile, arranged along the cracked driveway so that the space between the second and fifth approximated a parking spot. Dylan had objected at first, saying the driveway wasn't a street, and his grandfather had said nothing, only sat down on the porch step with his coffee and waited, which was his way of winning an argument without having one. That had been two weeks ago, at the start of summer, when the test was still an abstraction. Now it was Thursday, and the test was Saturday morning.

"You're not turning the wheel early enough," his grandfather said. "You wait until you're past the cone, then you turn."

Dylan eased backward between the cones, felt the car's rear swing wide, and stopped an inch from the fourth one. He had begun, somewhere in the second week, to parametrize the whole maneuver without meaning to: the angle of the first turn, the moment the wheel straightened, the depth of the space, each one a variable he could adjust. It worked better than thinking about it as a single scary thing. But the variables betrayed him whenever he rushed, and he rushed whenever he thought about Saturday, which meant he was rushing constantly.

David had already passed, first try, and had texted a photo of his temporary license with the caption "easy," a caption so pithy Dylan had almost thrown his phone into the hedges. Tristin had failed twice, both times on the highway portion, and had told Dylan over fries that the examiner, a woman named Ms. Han, watched your hands more than your eyes. Dylan wasn't sure this was true. Tristin said a lot of things with total certainty, and half of them turned out to be inventions, and the other half turned out to be warnings you wished you'd heeded.

After the cones, they drove. His grandfather lived at the edge of town where the county road fed onto the interstate, and the on-ramp was a long curve Dylan had ridden as a passenger maybe four hundred times without ever once considering it. Today he signaled, checked the mirror, and started up the ramp at thirty, intending to look for a gap and slip into it gently, the way you'd ease into a crowded hallway.

Behind him, a truck's horn sounded, long and furious. His grandfather's hand came down flat on the dashboard. "Go," he said. "Accelerate." Dylan pressed the pedal and the car climbed to fifty-five, sixty, and then there was a gap, and he was in it, moving with the traffic, and the truck passed harmlessly in the next lane. His hands were shaking on the wheel.

"You hesitated," his grandfather said, quieter now. "That lane is called the acceleration lane. You use it to get up close to highway speed before you merge." He looked out the window at the fields sliding past. "Coming in slow makes everyone brake. That's how you cause the accident you were trying to avoid."

Dylan held the car steady in the lane and thought about it. His whole instinct had been that caution looked like slowness, that being careful meant being small and tentative, waiting to be let in. But the ramp had offered him the opposite: safety was commitment. You matched the traffic, joined its speed, and then the merge was nothing. It was strange to him that the bold move and the safe move could be the same move, and he turned it over for several miles without deciding whether it applied to anything beyond driving. Probably it didn't. Probably it did.

They took the next exit and looped back, and this time Dylan was doing forty at the base of the ramp, sixty by the top, and slid into traffic so smoothly that his grandfather made a small sound, not quite approval and not quite surprise, and turned the radio up one notch. The afternoon light came slantwise across the hood. On the second loop they passed a roadside stand selling peaches, and on the third his grandfather bought a bag of them, and Dylan ate one at the wheel in the parking lot, juice running down his wrist, the fuzz of the skin still on his fingers when he signaled, checked his mirror, and pulled back onto the county road toward the house.

That evening he called Tristin, who had failed the highway portion twice and was scheduled for a third attempt the following month. "It's the ramp," Dylan said. "Don't crawl up it. Get to highway speed in the acceleration lane before you merge, because if you come in slow, everyone behind you has to brake." There was a pause on the line, the sound of Tristin deciding whether to believe him.

"You sure?" Tristin said.

Dylan looked out the window at the driveway, where the cones stood in the dusk exactly where they'd stood all summer, and he thought about Saturday, and about the fact that he had gotten it right twice out of three.

"Pretty sure," he said.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: On many ocean current maps, warm currents are drawn with red arrows and cold currents with blue arrows.
story:
Sarah spread the current map across the picnic table and weighted its corners with her mother's garden gnome, a cantaloupe, and two rocks, because the backyard wind had opinions about homework. The map was for her oceanography unit, and by Monday she had to be able to explain, out loud, in front of people, how the Gulf Stream kept northern Europe from freezing. She had read the textbook chapter twice and understood roughly one third of it, which she rounded up to half.

Jace dropped over the fence the way he always did, without warning, landing in the flowerbed and apologizing to the roses. He leaned over the map, squinting. "Okay, so the red ones are the fast ones, right? Red means fast. Like, the current's zooming."

Sarah looked at the red arrows sweeping up the Atlantic and then at the blue ones curling south, and something snagged in her mind. Jace sounded so confident, the way he sounded about everything, including the time he insisted possums laid eggs. "Fast seems weird, though," she said slowly. "Look at the blue ones off California. Some of those arrows are huge and long. Are they slow?"

"Big arrows, slow water," Jace said, as if this were obvious. "It's like the map is showing you the workout intensity."

She almost let it go. That was the thing about Jace's wrongness, it arrived dressed as common sense. But she flipped to the map's legend, that little box she'd skipped because legends looked like the boring part, and there it was in small print: warm currents drawn in red, cold currents in blue. Nothing about speed at all. "Jace. It's temperature. Warm currents are red arrows, cold currents are blue arrows."

He stared at the legend as if it had personally insulted his family. "So the Gulf Stream is red because it's warm, not because it's speedy."

"That's what it says."

"And I just told you it was speed with my whole chest." He sat down heavily on the bench, betrayed by cartography.

Sarah laughed, but her brain had already moved on, tracing the red arrow that ran from the Gulf of Mexico up along the American coast and then angled across toward Europe. Warm water, traveling north and east, toward places like Britain and Norway that sat at latitudes where, by rights, winters ought to be vicious. Her grandmother lived in Manchester and grew tomatoes. Sarah had never once wondered how. She wondered now, though the map alone didn't hand her the whole answer, and she could feel the edge of what she didn't yet know, the way the red arrow explained something without explaining everything.

She texted Abbey, who was at her grandmother's that weekend and had already declared herself Sarah's remote research assistant. "Ask your gran how cold Manchester winters actually are," Sarah typed, "compared to, like, Newfoundland, which is at the same latitude. Report back." Then, because Abbey demanded receipts: "Also Jace thought red arrows meant fast currents. Temperature, Abbey. The colors mean temperature."

The reply came twenty minutes later, and Sarah read it aloud to Jace, who had begun making a hat out of the cantaloupe's netting. "Gran says Manchester winters are damp and annoying but you can still grow things in November, and she had to look up Newfoundland on her globe because who thinks about Newfoundland, and up there it's apparently 'proper dour,' her words, sea ice and everything. She also says you're both ridiculous and I should tell Jace that a map legend is not optional reading. She signed it: from a dissident of the school of guessing. What does that even mean?"

"It means your gran is merciless," Jace said, "and I deserve it, and also I'm keeping this melon hat forever."

Ms. Delgado appeared at the fence that divided their yards, drawn out by the sound of their argument about whether damp counted as cold. She was a retired science teacher who watered her tomatoes with the unhurried patience of someone who had survived thirty years of teenagers, and she listened to Sarah's stumbling explanation, red arrow carrying warmth toward Europe, blue arrows carrying cold the other way, Manchester tomatoes versus Newfoundland ice, without correcting anything, which Sarah took as either a good sign or a trap.

"So the warmth gets delivered," Sarah finished, "like a shipping route, except the packages are degrees. But I can't tell from the map how much of the warming is the current and how much is other stuff, winds or whatever. The map makes it look tidy and it's probably not tidy."

Ms. Delgado smiled at that longer than at anything else and went back to her tomatoes. Sarah looked down at the red arrow crossing the Atlantic, the whole improbable delivery route of it, and got out her notebook to try the explanation again in her own words, while Jace, in his netting hat, read the legend out loud one more time, very slowly, like a man correcting the record.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The force on a charge in an electric field equals the charge times the field strength, F = qE, so doubling the charge doubles the force.
story:
The museum's electricity hall smelled like dust and hand sanitizer, and Addison had been standing in front of the parallel plate exhibit for eleven minutes before Jadyn finally said something about it.

"You're doing homework at a museum," Jadyn said. "That's a new level."

"I'm not doing homework." Addison pulled her notebook closer anyway. "Ms. Augustin said the exam would have one question like this. One. And nobody in class could do it."

The exhibit was simpler than she'd expected: two metal plates, pale and slightly grimy, mounted upright in a glass case with a dial that let visitors set the voltage between them. A printed card explained, in the museum's patient font, that a charged particle released between the plates would drift toward one side or the other. There was a button labeled DUST. When she pressed it, a puff of tiny particles floated into the gap and, sure enough, they slid sideways in a slow, even procession, like snow deciding on a direction.

River arrived with three churros, one already in his mouth. "Did you press the button? Press the button."

"I pressed the button," Jadyn said. "It's not that exciting."

"It's kind of exciting," Addison said, and surprised herself by meaning it.

She wrote down the numbers on the card. The plates were five centimeters apart. The dial was set to three hundred volts. Field strength, according to the formula Ms. Augustin had scrawled on the board before the bell, was voltage divided by distance. Three hundred divided by point zero five. She did it twice on the margin of her page and got six thousand newtons per coulomb both times, which felt like a lot, though she had no intuition for whether it was.

"Six thousand," she said out loud.

"Six thousand what?" River leaned over her shoulder, churro sugar drifting onto the page.

"Newtons per coulomb. The field strength between the plates." She squinted through the glass. "The card says the dust particles each carry about two nanocoulombs of charge. So I could figure out the actual force on one. The force on a charge in an electric field equals the charge times the field strength."

"Say that again like a person," Jadyn said.

"F equals q E. If I know the field, and I know the charge, I multiply them." She wrote it as she spoke, the way Ms. Augustin did, symbols first and sense later. Two nanocoulombs was two times ten to the minus nine. Times six thousand. She moved the decimal with her pen tip, checked it, checked it again. One point two times ten to the minus five newtons.

"Is that big?" River asked.

"No idea. But it's the push on one speck of dust." She looked at the drifting particles with something close to affection. They were being shoved by exactly that much, each of them, right now, and before today the number had not existed for her at all.

The dial had a second setting, marked PARTICLE CHARGE, that she hadn't touched. On a hunch she turned it from two nanocoulombs to four, doubling the charge, and pressed DUST again. The new particles crossed the gap faster. Not subtly faster, either. She watched one go, then did the arithmetic in her head: double the charge, double the force. Six thousand field, four nanocoulombs, two point four times ten to the minus five newtons. The second speck was being shoved exactly twice as hard as the first.

"So it's fair," she said.

"It's fair?" Jadyn repeated.
