"The field doesn't care what it's pushing. It pushes each charge in proportion to what the charge is. A bigger charge gets a bigger force, the same proportion, every time." She heard herself and winced a little. "That came out sounding like a fortune cookie."

"No, I get it," River said. "It's like, the rule treats everything the same, so the result is different but the rule isn't."

Jadyn squinted at the dial. "But wait. If you doubled the charge by turning a knob, isn't the exhibit just making it look that way? Like, it could be programmed to do anything. We're trusting a museum button."

Addison stopped writing. That was the thing about Jadyn that other people found exhausting and that Addison had decided, judiciously, years ago, to treat as a gift: she never let a conclusion survive on charm alone. Addison had once believed a boy in eighth grade who claimed he could desiccate a grape into a raisin using only a desk lamp and focus, and Jadyn had been the one to call him a charlatan, at length, in the cafeteria. She had been right. The grape had rotted.

"I don't know," Addison said. "The math works either way. F equals q E, so doubling q doubles F. But whether the dust is really doing that in there, or whether the button just speeds up a video, I can't tell from here."

"So write both," Jadyn said. "What you can prove and what you're taking on faith."

Addison looked at her page, at the two forces stacked in her handwriting, one exactly twice the other, and then through the glass at the particles still crossing in their slow straight lines. She pressed the button a third time.

"There," she said, and watched them go.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: All 50 US states and Washington, DC allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age.
story:
Elizabeth sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with three library books, a pizza box for a desk, and the strong suspicion that she had volunteered for a mistake. Her health class had been given the option of teaching a topic instead of being tested on it, and she had raised her hand before her brain could file an objection. Now she had to stand up on Thursday and explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested for infections at a clinic, to twenty-six classmates who had known her since she cried during the fourth-grade spelling bee over the word "receive."

"Receive has the i before the e except after c," said Miley from the bed, where she was lying upside down with her legs against the wall. "You're welcome. Historicize it. That's what Ms. Weiss said in English. Take your shame and put it in the past."

"Ms. Weiss said that about Hamlet." Elizabeth flipped a page. "Also, why are you upside down."

"Blood flow to the brain. I'm helping." Miley slid down until her head thumped softly on the rug. "Okay, tell me your thing. Practice on me. I'll be the class."

Elizabeth took a breath and began with consent, which turned out to be the part she could say best because it was mostly about paying attention. Enthusiastic yes, the absence of no isn't a yes, anyone can change their mind at any point, and being drunk is not a mood, it's a condition. Miley kept interrupting with questions that were actually good, which was annoying, because it meant Elizabeth couldn't just perform knowledge, she had to hold it.

The contraception section went worse. She had diagrams. Miley held one up to the light and said, "This looks like a satellite," and Elizabeth had to agree that it did, a little, and they laughed until her mother knocked on the door and asked if everything was all right, and Elizabeth said, "Homework," which was technically true and felt, in her mouth, like a small betrayal.

It was the third section that snagged her, the clinic part, and it snagged because of Alexus. Alexus had come over the week before, back when Elizabeth had first said yes to the presentation, and had gone quiet in a way Alexus never went quiet. Alexus, who once argued for twenty minutes at lunch that a hot dog could be a taco if you believed in it, had sat on the edge of Elizabeth's desk and said, not looking at her, "Could you even go somewhere? For a test. Wouldn't they call your mom for a form or something." Elizabeth had said she didn't know. She had thought about it since, at odd hours, folding the question like a note she couldn't deliver.

So on Tuesday, while Miley read magazines on the floor, Elizabeth called the county clinic. A nurse answered, brisk and unbothered, as though teenagers phoning about this were the most ordinary weather in the world. Elizabeth asked, feeling the question leave her like something physical, whether a parent had to sign.

"All fifty states and DC let minors consent to testing and treatment for STIs themselves," the nurse said. "No parent permission needed. Some states set a minimum age, but around here you're fine at seventeen." Elizabeth wrote it down twice, once in her notebook and once on the pizza box, as though the grease might preserve it better.

"You're grinning like a cartoon raccoon," Miley said.

"I found something out and now I have to tell Alexus."

She found Alexus at the lunch table on Wednesday, defending, as tradition demanded, some position about whether cereal was soup. Elizabeth sat down, waited through the ruling, and said quietly, "You don't need your mom's signature. Any state. Testing and treatment. Some states have a minimum age, but not one that touches you." Alexus went still, fork suspended, and Elizabeth watched the information land and rearrange something behind her eyes. "That changes things," Alexus said finally. "I thought it was a locked door. I'd kind of historicized it, you know? Decided it was just how the past was going to keep being."

"Ms. Weiss is leaking into all of us," said Miley, mournfully.

On Thursday Elizabeth stood at the front of the class with her diagrams, one of which still resembled a satellite, and told them about consent in plain words, and about contraception without blushing much, and about the clinic. She said the part about the states and about a parent not needing to sign, and she watched a girl in the second row, dour all semester, chin resting on her fist, lift her head an inch. She said, too, that she hadn't known any of it two weeks ago, that you could carry a fact like a coin in your shoe and feel it every step, and that some things, like what you owe the people you care about and how to say the awkward true thing, she was still figuring out. The clock above the door showed two minutes left.

Ms. Weiss, who taught English but had drifted in to watch, raised her hand from the back. "One question. Is a hot dog a sandwich?"

"That's Alexus's department," said Elizabeth, and Alexus stood up.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the traditional colour wheel, like red and green, and placed side by side they make each other look brighter.
story:
Jordan had promised Mr. Yang a full formal critique of a Frida Kahlo painting by Friday, and it was Wednesday evening, and he had written one sentence. The sentence was "The painting is very green," which he had already crossed out twice and rewritten once, and which the woman at the front desk of the community art studio had read over his shoulder and pronounced "a strong start." Her name tag said she volunteered on Wednesdays and hated painters who chewed their brushes, so Jordan kept his brush far from his mouth.

Marina had commandeered the table by the window, where the light was best and the radiators made the least noise. She was supposed to be helping him, though so far her contribution had been to draw a small top hat on the reproduction of Kahlo's self-portrait that Jordan had printed out. "It's symbolic," she said, when he objected. "Of how you've learned nothing."

"I've learned things. The composition, for instance." He turned the print so the hat faced away from him. "She puts herself dead center, staring out, and the background wraps around her like a frame. The monkey, the cat, the leaves. Everything closes in."

"That's not nothing," Marina admitted. "Now do color."

The problem was the color, or rather the problem was that the color was doing something to his eyes that he could not name. Around the figure's face, the red of a ribbon or a flower sat pressed right against the green of the jungle leaves, and where they touched, both seemed to intensify, to hum, as if each were shouting to be noticed over the other. He said as much to Marina, squinting at the print, and Craig, who had arrived late with two granola bars and no visible intention of doing art, leaned over and looked.

Craig, it turned out, had spent an entire semester of design class being torpid in the back row while the teacher drilled the color wheel into everyone else. "Complementary colours," he said, with his mouth full. "They sit opposite each other on the traditional colour wheel, like red and green. Put them side by side and they make each other look brighter." He shrugged, as if embarrassed to be useful. "She makes you paint stripes about it. Mine were ugly."

Jordan wrote it down before Craig could get modest about it. So the vibrating edge was not an accident, not a trick of the cheap print, not his tired eyes. Kahlo had chosen it. He tried to work out why, sketching a quick diagram of the painting on the studio's scrap paper: the figure centered, the reds clustered near the face, the greens spreading outward to swallow the frame. The red announced the body, the living, blood-warm self, and the green crowded it on every side, dense and watchful. The brightness where they met was the whole argument of the painting, the self lit up by everything pressing against it.

"It's like apportionment," Marina said, peering at his diagram. "She gives out the color in careful amounts. A little red, a lot of green, and the smallness of the red is why it matters so much."

"That's better than my top hat," Craig said.

"It's not a competition." Marina drew a second, smaller top hat on the diagram.

Jordan kept writing until the studio's closing announcement crackled through the PA, which the volunteer woman delivered with the joy of someone reading a hostage statement. He had three pages now, and a real critique shaping up underneath them, but a knot remained at the center that he could not smooth away. He believed the color was doing what he said it was doing, and he believed the monkey and the thorn necklace were symbols, but he could not prove that Kahlo meant it the way he was claiming, and every time he wrote "clearly," he heard Mr. Yang's voice saying, clearly to whom. He might be right. He might be aggrandizing a painter's practical choice into a grand statement about the self. There was no way to know from a printout in a community studio on a Wednesday night.

Marina packed up his pencils for him, since he was still writing. Craig left one granola bar on the table without comment. At the door, the volunteer woman said, "Strong start," and Jordan, holding three pages and one honest uncertainty, said, "I'll finish it tomorrow," and she flipped the light switch on him mid-syllable.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The square graduation cap is called a mortarboard because it resembles the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar.
story:
The wind came off the football field in long, patient gusts, and Oliver's cap lifted off his head for the third time in ten minutes. He caught it both times before, but this time it went high enough that Eamon had to snatch it out of the air like a frisbee, and a woman in the folding-chair section laughed at them, not unkindly.

"I don't understand why it's shaped like this," Oliver said, taking it back. "It's a square. A flat square. Whoever designed a hat that's basically a shelf."

"Processional starts in eight minutes," Francois said. He was holding the printed program stiffly, as if it were an assignment he intended to hand in early. "You're going to fight the aerodynamics of your own hat for eight minutes?"

Eamon already had his phone out, because Eamon always already had his phone out. He scrolled with his thumb, shielding the screen from the sun. "Okay, it's called a mortarboard," he said. "Because it looks like the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar."

Oliver stood with the cap in both hands and let that land. A bricklayer's board. Somebody had looked at a tool for carrying paste between bricks and thought, yes, that, but on a seventeen-year-old's head. He turned the cap over. The tassel hung from a button at the center, and underneath, where his skull was supposed to go, there was a soft crown of cloth holding almost nothing in place.

"Great," Francois said. "So we're all dressed as masons."

"There's something in that," Oliver said, and Eamon groaned, but Oliver kept going anyway, because the thought would not wait. "The whole thing is built, right. School, the ceremony, the caps. Somebody lays it brick by brick and tells you it was always a wall." He was thinking of his father, who had emailed him a link two nights ago to a summer internship at the logistics firm, subject line blank, body text only "Say yes by Friday." Friday had become this morning, and this morning had become now, and the deadline sat in his phone unanswered while he stood in a rented gown on a soccer field.

Ms. Sokolov found them near the edge of the graduating class, doing the rounds with the weary efficiency of a woman who had attended twenty-six of these ceremonies and still bothered to learn names. "Mr. Adeyemi," she said. "Your essay on the Tacitus translation was the one I actually kept."

"That's the one you gave me a B on," Oliver said.

"The B was for the conclusion," she said. "You resolved an argument you hadn't finished having." She straightened a boy's collar beside him without breaking eye contact. "The world will let you reify that habit if you let it. Everything becomes a thing you can hold, and then you stop asking whether it should exist."

She moved on down the line, and Francois leaned in. "What does that mean, though."

"It means she wants me to say no to my dad," Oliver said. Except he wasn't sure that was true. His father had come to this country with one duffel bag and a cosmopolitan fluency in three languages he had taught himself on night shifts, and when his father said the internship was steady, that was not small thinking. That was sagacity earned in a way Oliver's had not been. Ms. Sokolov had books and deadlines and a certainty that a mind should stay open. His father had a certainty that a life had to close around something eventually, and Oliver could not honestly say which certainty had been more expensive to acquire.

Five minutes. The wind picked up again, and the whole front row of graduates grabbed at their heads at once, a wave of hands and square boards, mortar threatening to spill. Oliver put his on and pressed the crown down hard, then took it off again. He pulled the stiff cardboard square free of the cloth, turned it over in his hands, and slid it back in at an angle that let the crown sit deeper, lower, snug against his skull. It held. It would probably hold through the whole ceremony, and if it didn't, he would catch it.

The band started tuning. He took out his phone and typed to his father, then deleted it, then typed again. He held his thumb over send while the first rows began to move, Eamon tugging his sleeve, Francois already three steps ahead with his program held high like a ticket.

"Coming or not?" Eamon called.

Oliver looked at the screen, then at the field, then put the phone in his pocket unanswered and stepped into line with the cap riding low and sure on his head.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould.
story:
Audrey turned the thermostat dial on the double boiler down a degree and watched the thermometer slip past ninety-two, then ninety, then eighty-eight, the dark chocolate moving in slow, glossy folds beneath the spatula. Tomorrow afternoon her mother's retirement party would fill the backyard with forty coworkers, and Audrey had promised two hundred moulded chocolates, a promise she had made before she had ever successfully tempered a single batch.

"You're stirring like it owes you money," Larry said from the counter, where he was wiping polycarbonate moulds with a cotton ball until they squeaked. He had come over at eight in the morning with a bag of apricots and no other plans, which was the kind of friend he was.

"It has to reach a temperature and then come back up a little," Audrey said. "That's all I know. The internet gave me numbers but not reasons. Seed, melt, test on the back of a spoon. If the spoon sets shiny in five minutes, it's in temper." She lifted the bowl and let a ribbon of chocolate fall back in, reading the way it folded, whether it held a moment before sinking. Everything about it seemed like a language she could almost hear.

Denis arrived at ten with his own moulds and his own bowl, already half full of chocolate he had melted straight in the microwave. "Same thing, faster," he said, tapping the mould on the counter to settle his first filled cavities. "Chocolate's chocolate." Audrey looked at his bowl and noticed it wasn't holding a ribbon at all; it poured like warm syrup and kept a dull sheen on the surface, but she said nothing, because she wasn't sure enough yet to say it, and because Denis had brought the apricots she needed for her ganache.

By noon the kitchen smelled like a bakery's idea of heaven. Audrey's test spoon had set in four minutes with a satin finish and a clean edge, so she filled her moulds in careful passes, scraping the surface flat with a bench knife, and slid them into the cool pantry. Then she and Larry boiled cream for the filling and argued about whether a recipe was a rule or a suggestion. "A recipe codifies what worked for one person on one day," Larry said, waving the wooden spoon. "You still have to taste it yourself." Audrey thought that was the most intelligent thing anyone had said in her kitchen all year, and told him so, which made him insufferable for the rest of the hour.

Denis's trouble began at two. He turned his first mould over and tapped it, and nothing came out. He tapped harder. Two chocolates released with torn, streaked tops, and the rest sat in their cavities like things with a grudge. "These moulds are defective," he announced, holding one up to the window light, and Audrey took it from him and looked at the chocolate that refused to move. She looked at the mould, then at her own first tray in the pantry, which had been setting for an hour and a half.

She carried her tray out and turned it upside down over the parchment, and before she even tapped, she felt the chocolate shift, loose in its cells. One gentle knock and twenty-four identical shells dropped out in rows, each with a hard shine and edges so crisp they looked cut. She picked one up and snapped it in two beside her ear, and it broke with a sound like a small dry twig. "Tempered chocolate shrinks a little as it sets," she said slowly, still looking at the halves, "and that's why it comes out of the mould clean." She held up Denis's ruined tray beside hers. "Yours never shrank. Yours was never in temper at all."

Denis stared at his mould, then at the microwave, and had the grace to say nothing about defective equipment. There were four hours left before the chocolates had to be done, and Denis's chocolate had to be reworked from the beginning, taken up hot and brought back down, and Audrey wondered whether it was strange that she felt almost grateful for his failure, because now she understood something she had only followed instructions about. The kitchen was a mess, the cream had scorched once, and they were going to be profligate with the remaining chocolate because there was no time to be careful twice. She handed Denis her thermometer and a fresh bag of couverture.

"If it works this time," Denis said, stirring, "I'm taking credit for the scientific method." Larry snorted, and Audrey lifted her second tray of filled moulds toward the pantry, watching the chocolate catch the overhead light on its way past, each surface holding a small bright image of the room. "You can take credit for the moulds being clean," she said, and closed the pantry door on them all.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In 1859, John Tyndall began laboratory experiments measuring how gases absorb infrared heat, showing that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb it while nitrogen and oxygen do not.
story:
The trail to the campsite wound through pines that had been dying for years, their trunks gray and stripped, and Marcus counted them out of habit until the counting felt like something he should not be doing. He carried the food bag because his father had claimed the tent, and behind him Hazel carried her own pack with the exaggerated patience of someone who had already decided the weekend was going to be tedious. Marcus had a report due when he got home, three pages on carbon dioxide, and he had brought the graph folded into his jacket pocket, which Hazel had mocked twice since the parking lot.

"You brought homework to the woods," she said at the fire ring, after they had set up and the light was going amber behind the ridge.

"It's one graph," Marcus said. "It's not homework homework. It's a thing I don't understand and it's bugging me."

That was not exactly true. What bugged him was that his draft had come back from Ms. Ortiz with a single note in the margin, in her small handwriting: You're repeating something. Find where it started. He had read the note eight times. He knew how to repeat things; he had gotten good grades for years by repeating things well. He did not know how to find where something started.

His father built the fire with the gravity of a man performing a ritual, arranging the kindling in a lattice, and Marcus watched the flames catch and thought, without wanting to, about heat. That was the problem with reading about a subject for a week: it followed you. The fire radiated warmth onto his face while the air behind his head stayed cold, and he caught himself wondering why the heat came at him in a straight line and did not seem to linger in the air between them.

Hazel was telling a story about Britany, who had apparently tried to return a rented kayak while it was still tied to the roof of her car, and their father laughed in a way that invigorated the whole campsite, the sound rolling up the slope. Marcus laughed too. But later, when the fire had burned down to a red architecture of coals and his father had gone to the tent, he took the graph out of his pocket and flattened it on the picnic table.

Hazel sat across from him with a mug of something that steamed. "Show me," she said, in the tone of someone humoring a younger sibling, though they were the same age.

The graph was simple enough once you learned to read it. A line climbing from left to right across a century, low and nearly flat and then bending steeply upward in the last decades, like a road that had been level and then discovered a mountain. He had stared at it at his desk at home without it meaning anything. Here, under the propane lantern, with the coals still throwing heat, it began to mean something. He put his finger on the flat part.

"This is basically my great-grandparents," he said. "This bend here is my parents. This last bit is us."

"Cheerful," Hazel said.

He had also brought a printout of something he had found at two in the morning, a page he had almost not printed because it seemed wrong, like citing a source that could not possibly be real. He smoothed it open. In 1859 a man named John Tyndall had begun laboratory experiments, measuring how gases absorb infrared heat. That was the phrase, infrared heat, and Marcus had looked up infrared and found only that it was heat radiation, which was not helpful, so he had stopped looking. What the experiments had shown was the strange part. Water vapor and carbon dioxide absorbed the heat. Nitrogen and oxygen did not.

"Wait," Hazel said, leaning over the table with her mug forgotten. "They figured that out in 1859? Before cars? I thought the whole greenhouse thing was, like, modern. Eighties."

"That's what I thought." He had assumed the greenhouse effect was an invention of the late twentieth century, something that had arrived with satellites and anxiety, and finding a Victorian gentleman with laboratory equipment behind it had rearranged something in his head. It was not a new idea being argued into existence. It was an old measurement, sitting there for more than a century and a half while the line on the graph bent upward.

"So your report is about the experiment?" his father's voice said from the tent flap, and Marcus had not realized he was listening. His father came out in his coat and sat down, and there was a moment where the subtext became legible to Marcus: his father, who drove a delivery route and called climate talk a political industry, was asking in a neutral voice about a laboratory in 1859, about a man with instruments, because that was apparently a different thing than a lecture. Marcus understood suddenly that the gravitas of a graph came from where it started, and that the number bending upward meant something different when you knew the physics underneath it had been measured before anyone had a stake in it.

"I don't know what it's about yet," Marcus said, which was honest. He knew the line climbed. He knew the coals were hot and the air was not. He knew water vapor and carbon dioxide absorbed infrared heat and nitrogen and oxygen did not, and he did not know, in the way Ms. Ortiz would want him to know, what exactly he believed followed from all of it, or how much of the bending line was ours and how much was the world doing what the world does. He said some of that out loud, and his father nodded slowly, and Hazel pulled the graph toward herself and traced the curve with one finger, back down from the top to the flat beginning, as if checking whether it had always been going somewhere.

The lantern hissed. Somewhere below the ridge, water moved over stones.

"This is the part that's us," Hazel said, tapping the steep end of the line.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: A few drops of water in melted chocolate can make it seize into a thick, grainy paste, because the sugar and cocoa particles clump together.
story:
Violet had promised Ms. Clarke she would run the stall alone on Saturday, which meant forty truffles, a folding table, and a hand-lettered sign reading DARK CHOCOLATE, TEMPERED PROPERLY, whatever properly meant. All summer Ms. Clarke had been trying to inculcate the habits of a confectioner into her: the clean bowls, the dry spoon, the thermometer warmed in her palm before it touched the chocolate. Violet had absorbed most of it the way she absorbed most things, reluctantly and then all at once. The tempering, though, still felt like weather, something that happened to her rather than something she did.

She set up the double boiler behind the table, between the crates of waxed paper and the cash box. Eleonore arrived at eight with two coffees and no plans to leave. "You're doing the seed method," Eleonore said, reading the index card Violet had taped to the table leg. "This says stir for ten minutes. That's pedantry, isn't it? Ten minutes, eleven minutes, who could tell the difference."

"The chocolate could," Violet said, but she said it without conviction, because she honestly didn't know. She had succeeded twice at home and failed once, and she could not have said what she had done differently.

The morning was cool for July, which was a mercy, and the market filled slowly: the peach vendor calling out grades, a man testing every jar of honey with the same suspicious spoon, children orbiting the bread stand. Charles-Antoine came by on his way to shift a piano for his uncle and stayed twenty minutes arguing with Eleonore about whether tempering was chemistry or cooking. He said chemistry. Eleonore said cooking was just chemistry you were allowed to eat. Violet, stirring, said nothing, because the chocolate had reached temperature and the next five minutes were the ones that mattered, and because she suspected the argument was really about something else, something the two of them had been circling since June.

She stirred. She added the seed chocolate, chopped fine, and watched it melt down and drag the temperature with it. Ms. Clarke's voice was in her head, not the incisive way she spoke in the kitchen but the softer way she spoke after, saying that tempering was a matter of alignment, that the crystals wanted to form a certain way and your job was mostly to stop interfering. Violet had found that almost useless as instruction and completely true as description, which was the story of everything Ms. Clarke had ever taught her.

Then it happened. The saucepan had been simmering too hard, and the lid she'd set loosely over the water had gathered steam along its underside, and when she nudged it aside to check the flame, three or four drops ran off the edge and into the bowl. Not much. Barely a splash. But the chocolate changed in the time it took her to draw a breath: it went stiff, thickened against the spoon, turned dull and grainy, a paste rather than a liquid. She stopped stirring. The whole morning, forty truffles, the sign, all of it was sitting in that bowl in a changed state.

"What did you do?" Charles-Antoine asked.

"Nothing. I didn't do anything." But she had, or the water had, and she stood there holding the spoon and thinking back through Ms. Clarke's warnings, which she had filed under superstition: dry bowl, dry spoon, wipe the bottom of the bowl, keep the lid offset. A few drops of water, Ms. Clarke had said once, and Violet hadn't believed that so little could undo so much. "It seized," she said, and the word came back to her the way words do, arriving with the thing attached. "Water got in. It seizes. That's what it's called."

Eleonore leaned over the bowl and poked the surface with one finger. "It looks like wet sand. That's completely ruined?"

"Completely." Violet scraped at it with the spoon and the mass clung and held, grainy as brown sugar. There was a way to rescue it, she thought, cream or something, which turned it into ganache, which was a different product, which was not what the sign said.

She stood with her hands on the table edge and did the math. It was nine-forty. The chocolate shop on Delacroix opened at ten and sold the same couverture she was using, and if she ran, she could be back by ten past, and the tempering would take twenty minutes if it worked, and the market's real rush came at eleven. It could work. It could also not work, and she'd be out forty dollars of chocolate with nothing to show.

"Go," Eleonore said. "We'll hold the table. Charles-Antoine, you're not moving a piano, you're watching me sell nothing."

"Excuse me, truffles," Charles-Antoine said, "are nothing? These are—" He held up one of the display samples Violet had made at home, the good ones, glossy, and put it back. "These are something."

Violet ran. She ran past the peach vendor and the honey man and the bread stand, past Ms. Clarke, who was buying plums three stalls down and called out something she didn't catch, and she thought, as she ran, that next week she would use a bowl suspended on a clip above the water with no lid anywhere near it, and that she would never again mistake a careful instruction for pedantry. She'd have to tell Ms. Clarke the whole thing honestly, the steam, the lid, the drops, and she was already composing the sentence. At the shop door she stopped, breathless, coins counted in her fist, and found Ms. Clarke beside her, holding out a bar of her own. "Delacroix's is out on Saturdays," she said. "I know the hours. Run back, I'll come."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Circumlocution, describing a word you cannot remember instead of stopping, is a recognized communication strategy that keeps a second-language speaker talking.
story:
The topic was drawn from a bowl at the front of the room, folded twice, and read aloud by Mr. Mercado with the flat ceremony of a judge: whether the city should raise the transit tax to fund free bus fare for students. Hailey had five minutes, entirely in Spanish, and no notes. She had two nights to prepare, and her position, which was the actual problem, kept refusing to become a single position.

At the kitchen table she argued both sides to nobody. A higher tax took remuneration, in tiny amounts, from everyone who drove, and gave it to kids who rode; that was one story, clean and generous. But the same tax took from people who earned very little, and the school's own statistics pamphlet called that regressive, a word she liked the weight of. She wrote both columns in her notebook and then sat looking at them, wondering whether a person was allowed to hold two opinions at once, or whether that was just failure to choose.

On Thursday, Nyla sent her a message: "Practiced my debate and forgot the word for pollution at minute two and just stood there like a lamp. Do not be a lamp. Also Mr. Mercado says the timer doesn't stop, so whatever happens you have to keep going." Hailey read it twice, then once more. Keep going. She typed back a thumbs up, which felt noncommittal even to her, and turned to the mirror to try her opening line aloud. "El impuesto sobre el transporte," she said, and the phrase came out whole and sure, and she thought, wrongly, that this was the hard part.

Friday, Room 114, third period. Mr. Mercado set a kitchen timer on the desk and clicked it. Hailey stood, said her opening, and reached minute two without disaster. Then, reaching for the sentence she had rehearsed most, the sentence that carried her whole first argument, she found that impuesto had gone. The word for tax, the subject of the debate, the center of the topic itself, simply was not in her head anymore. The class waited. Nyla, in the second row, mouthed something she couldn't read.

"So the plan asks everyone who drives to pay a little more money," Hailey said in Spanish, slowly, "this money that the government takes from people, not because they did something wrong, but to pay for things we all use." She heard herself doing it and almost faltered out of surprise. She kept the rhythm. "This money, you pay it when you buy gasoline," she added, and a boy near the window nodded, and she realized he had understood, that she had built a bridge out of nothing and crossed it in front of everyone.

She hit the second argument, the regressive one, with a question she hadn't planned: "But is it fair to ask a person who earns little to give the same as a person who earns much? Some would impute bad motives to the city, saying it wants only to look generous. I don't think that. I think the plan is kind and also that it is unfair, and I don't yet know which matters more." The timer buzzed. Mr. Mercado wrote something without looking up. Kyleigh, on the opposite bench for rebuttal, opened her mouth and then closed it, which felt like its own kind of verdict.

Afterward, packing her bag, Hailey heard Nyla say to Kyleigh, "That thing she did, when she forgot the word? Circumlocution. My cousin's whole language school teaches it, describing around a word instead of stopping. It's a real strategy, not just panicking in style." Kyleigh said it sounded like cheating. Nyla said it sounded like talking. Hailey zipped her bag and thought about the difference, and couldn't find one she believed in, and found she didn't mind.

Mr. Mercado caught her at the door. "Your conclusion," he said. "You admitted uncertainty. Most students hide it." He handed back her notecard, untouched, which she had never once looked at. Outside, the buses were running up and down the avenue, free for now to nobody, paid for by nobody, and she watched one go by and wondered what she would say about it next week, and whether she would still be of two minds, and whether that was the thing to fix or the thing to keep.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: The genetic code is read in codons of three bases; there are 64 possible codons but only 20 standard amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon.
story:
The codon chart Ms. Xu had left on the front bench was the size of a placemat, and Sophie had been staring at it for eleven minutes without writing anything down. The retake was Thursday. On the original test she had written, in the margin of the translation question, that DNA gets copied into RNA and then RNA gets read to build a protein, which was true enough that Ms. Xu had given her two points out of ten, and not true enough for the B minus she needed to stay on the team roster for the regional quiz.

"You're doing the thing," Amina said from the next stool. She was cutting out paper bases with the little scissors from the drawer, building a model no one had asked her to build. "The staring thing. It never ends well."

"I'm not staring. I'm reading."

"You're reading the same square you read five minutes ago."

Magaly came in late, which was unlike her, and set her binder down harder than necessary. Magaly had the highest mark in the class going into this unit, and everyone knew she wanted the single lab assistant position Ms. Xu awarded in the spring, the one that mattered for early admissions. Sophie wanted it too, though she had told no one that, and had almost convinced herself it wasn't why she was here on a Tuesday afternoon with her failed test flattened under her elbow.

They ran the practice problems in silence after that. Sophie transcribed her sequence, checked it twice, then translated it base by base down the chart, sliding her finger along the rows. GGU. Her finger stopped on glycine. Fine. GGA. She moved to find the next amino acid, then moved back, because something was wrong with the chart, or wrong with her. She looked at GGU again. She looked at GGA again. Both of them landed on glycine. She checked GGC. Glycine. GGG. Glycine, again, four times over, and the hair on her arms lifted in the way it did when a locked door turned out to be open.

"Ms. Xu marked this wrong," she said slowly. She pulled the old test from under her elbow and smoothed it on the bench. Question six: the last codon of the sequence was GGA, and Sophie had written glycine, and there was red ink beside it, a single slash, and the letters "see key." She had assumed the slash meant she was wrong. She had assumed it for a week.

Magaly leaned over, and her face did something complicated. "That's the answer key's fault. The key only lists one codon per amino acid. I noticed it when I was checking my own test." A pause, the length of a held breath. "I didn't say anything."

"Why not?"

"Because you'd get the points back." Magaly said it flatly, without apology, and then began gathering her binder as though the sentence had been nothing. Amina's scissors had gone quiet. The overhead fan turned, and somewhere down the hall a door closed.

Sophie did the arithmetic on the back of her hand, where she did all her arithmetic. Four bases, read in groups of three, which meant four times four times four possible codons, sixty-four of them, and the chart's right-hand column kept collapsing into the same twenty amino acids over and over, serine four deep, leucine stacked like coins. Sixty-four doors into twenty rooms. She had spent a week believing she was wrong when she had been right, and the believing had been the whole injury, because she hadn't checked. She had let one red slash exonerate the key instead of herself.

"So Thursday I'm fine," she said. "I understand it now. It's not a code where every word means one thing, it's a code with... I don't know, slack in it." She had been treating translation like a lookup, a heuristic that worked for most of the test and then quietly betrayed her, and the honest thing was to admit she still didn't know why the slack existed, only that it did, and that her job Thursday was to read what was actually on the chart rather than what she expected.

She picked up the old test and walked it to the front bench, where Ms. Xu was watering the fern that had survived four years of sophomores. "Question six," Sophie said, and laid the paper down, and put her finger on GGA, and waited.

Magaly, at the door with her binder hugged to her chest, watched them both with her saturnine, unreadable eyes, and did not leave.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: The '10 percent rule', never raising weekly running distance more than 10 percent, is a popular guideline, but studies have not shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans.
story:
Amy taped the grid to the inside of her locker door on Monday: seven columns, seven rows, every cell blank except the two that said REST in block capitals. She had been named captain of the fall team in June, and Mr. Ortiz had told her, in his flat way, that captains at their school wrote the summer training plan. He handed her a key to the equipment shed and nothing else.

She met Graham on the field at seven the next morning, before the heat. He was already stretching in the grass with his ankle taped, because he had rolled it in May, and Amy crouched beside him with the clipboard.

"I'm building the plan around the ten percent rule," she said. "You never raise your weekly mileage more than ten percent from the week before."

"Who decided that?"

"Everybody. It's like a law." She wrote 20 miles in the first week's cell, then 22, then 24.2, working the percentages out on the margin. Graham watched the numbers climb and said nothing. His want was simpler than hers: he wanted to play the whole season without tape, and he said so, twice, on the walk to the water jugs.

Pablo changed everything on Thursday. He arrived at the field with his laptop because his family's wifi was out, and while Amy ran cones he sat on the bench reading, and when she came over, sweating, he turned the screen toward her. He had looked up the ten percent rule, out of boredom, out of the particular ennui of a boy watching other people train, and what he found was a stack of studies. He read the relevant sentence aloud, slowly, twice.

"Studies have not shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans," he said. "Other gradual plans. So it's a guideline, not a law."

Amy sat down on the bench. She stared at her grid, at the neat column of percentages she had calculated with such care, and felt something in her go quiet. The rule had catalyzed the whole plan; now it turned out the catalyst was just one option among several, and she had been treating it like gravity.

"So what do I do," she said, "throw it out?"

"No," Pablo said. "It's still gradual. It's still a ceiling. Just don't act like it's the only one."

She worked on it that evening at the picnic table behind the equipment shed, where Mr. Ortiz was inflating a rack of balls with a hand pump. She rebuilt the plan twice. The first version was spartan, almost punishing: distances, sprints, one rest day, no variation, as if discipline alone could substitute for knowing what she was doing. She looked at it and did not like it, so she started over. The second version kept the ten percent increases, because they were gradual and she understood them, but she added a cutback week every fourth week, dropped the Thursday session to warm-ups and ball work only, and penciled in a second rest day for anyone carrying an injury, which meant Graham. She could not say whether the cutback weeks were better. She only knew that both plans were gradual, and that one of them gave people room to be human.

On Saturday she brought both versions to the field and laid them side by side on the grass while Graham and Pablo and eleven others stood in a loose ring around her, Cleats scuffing the dirt, someone's water bottle hissing as it was squeezed. She told them the truth: that the ten percent rule was what she had, that she had believed it was law and found out it was not, that she could not promise this plan would keep anyone healthier than another one.

"Nobody's done the study that says ours is right," she said. "So we're guessing carefully. Week one starts Monday. Warm-ups first, then the cones."

Graham bent down, picked up the second plan, folded it once, and put it in the back pocket of his shorts. "This one," he said, and jogged out to the far goal to start his tape.
